Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 20: Tottenham
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 6th (NB: this is not necessarily John Brewin’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 17th

Prospects

Tottenham’s hopes for the season can be measured by what went wrong last season. And the season before that. This time last year, the arrival of a fresh, enthusiastic face in Thomas Frank gave considerable grounds for optimism. Surely Spurs would not be as bad in the Premier League as they had been in 2024-25? They proved to be worse. Despite a decent enough Champions League group stage, European football did not provide salvation for an ill-fitting manager or the unconvincing hierarchy around him.

That Frank is almost a forgotten figure owes much to the Igor Tudor interlude, a misadventure that resembled a disaster movie. Tottenham were on the brink of relegation until the season’s final days, a saga that became irresistible to rubberneckers. Roberto De Zerbi’s appointment was a much-needed corrective, the change in direction Spurs supporters clamoured for during so many years of their club never paying top dollar, of cutting corners. The Italian’s high wages were not his only demands. Fuller control than his predecessors, far more than he enjoyed at Brighton and Marseille, and a proper transfer spend on readymade players were also demanded. He has received them, though the lack of a top-level striker is glaring.

Thus, the unusual sensation of Tottenham being among the transfer window’s biggest spenders. Buying Jan Paul van Hecke, Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali, with Savinho and Omar Marmoush expected to also arrive from Manchester City, resembles the type of outlay rarely seen since Terry Venables was collecting Paul Gascoigne and Gary Lineker at White Hart Lane in the late 1980s or the influx of foreign talent in the mid-1990s – Jürgen Klinsmann, Ilie Dumitrescu and all that: a flash of glamour that is old-school Spurs. Andy Robertson’s addition as an experienced head is a further pointer towards a different Tottenham, one where success is expected and not promised, a very different form of optimism. Cristian Romero has departed, a player of talent whose foibles often betrayed his teammates, endemic of the Spurs era he played in.

Off-field picture

Finishing 17th two seasons in succession is bad for the bank balance. The club’s 2025 accounts revealed that the £34.7m garnered from winning the Europa League was wiped out by a £38.9m shortfall in Premier League income. Champions League football last season will help, with £71.6m trousered, but there are no European funds to feed off this season. The international break in September allows Tottenham Hotspur Stadium to welcome Jay-Z, having hosted the veteran heavy metal band System Of A Down in July. Two NFL regular season matches will be staged in October. Such revenue streams cushion Spurs, as does an August share issue that raised £100m.

Owner-fan relationship

The removal of Daniel Levy was what many Spurs fans had desired, but it also created a vacuum. The family trust of the former majority shareholder, Joe Lewis, took the residual heat. In January, Lewis’s daughter, Vivienne, was confronted by a fan demanding that Frank be sacked and that she sell up. The Lewis trust has doubled down. Levy’s 29% previous share is reduced by his missing the deadline for that August share issue; the two parties are reported to be battling over an NBA Europe franchise. Vinai Venkatesham, a chief executive who came under heavy fire, admitted in May “a complete reset” was required. Supporters will wait to gauge the success of the brave new world.

The manager

De Zerbi’s coaching is admired across the football spectrum, Pep Guardiola a confirmed fan, though breakdowns in relationships at both Brighton and Marseille offer caution. Will he be remembered solely for saving Spurs from relegation or can he offer progress in a fashion not seen since Mauricio Pochettino arrived in 2014? He has offered notes of realism to temper the excitement of the spending spree. “We need to create a clear playing style and give a soul to this team,” the Italian said in pre-season. “So many talk about ‘projects’, but very few manage to see them through.” He has been handed as blank a canvas as is available at any major club.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen João Pedro (left) and Dário Essugo (right) try to stop Spurs’ Sandro Tonali in his tracks during the 2-1 victory over Chelsea in their Sydney Cup friendly, in which Tonali opened the scoring. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PA

“The gaffer was Italian, I knew him,” was among the reasons Sandro Tonali offered for choosing Tottenham when a number of other suitors came calling. “I was already watching Tonali when he was playing for Brescia, my hometown club and the team I support,” explained De Zerbi. “At the age of 18, he already looked like a veteran.” With Tonali 26, Spurs have signed a peak-age player who, the season before last, was among the very best midfielders in English football, though his final season at Newcastle was mixed. A fee of £100m could not be refused.

Stat attack

Tottenham were the only club in the Premier League who overachieved their xG in attack by at least four while also underachieving by that margin or more in defence. It was up front where the biggest discrepancy occurred, with Spurs scoring 7.91 goals more than their chances implied they deserved. They might have been playing Championship football this season had this not happened.

Set for a breakthrough

Much is expected of Mikey Moore, though he is likely to go out on loan again after a season at Rangers. Antonin Kinsky was the victim of one of the horrors of the Tudor reign, subbed off after 17 minutes against Atlético Madrid, only to be trusted by the new manager as relegation was avoided. His save from Leeds’ Sean Longstaff was highly significant in the clamber to safety. Kinsky is set to be first choice this season after the departure of Guglielmo Vicario. “He forces you to believe in yourself,” said Kinsky of De Zerbi, who in turn said: “He has great personality, strong character.”

World Cup impact

Full-backs were Tottenham’s leading men in the United States. Djed Spence has departed for Inter but Pedro Porro remains, after signing a new deal amid interest from Manchester City. Porro scored twice, including in Spain’s semi-final defeat of France. As a world champion, the 26-year-old received a guard of honour on his return to his club’s training ground, having beaten the Argentina team of the now-departed Romero in the final. Among Tottenham’s nine players in North America, the new central defensive pairing of Van Hecke and Micky van de Ven was kept apart, the latter playing left-back as the Dutch disappointed.

Sports.title: Uefa and Concacaf discuss joint Nations League in latest challenge to Fifa
Sports.content:
Uefa and Concacaf have begun talks about setting up a combined Nations League tournament featuring all 96 European and North and Central American and Caribbean countries, in another direct challenge to Fifa.

The Guardian has learned that having come together to push for Gianni Infantino’s removal in the light of the World Cup sell-off controversy, the two confederations are now working on creating their own biennial tournament, which could launch as early as 2028 after the next European Championship.

Although discussions are at an early stage, it is understood the new competition would mirror the current multi-league format used for the existing Nations Leagues by Europe’s governing body and Concacaf, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football. It would be followed by a knockout phase, a final-four tournament to determine the champions.

League A would feature the top teams in Europe, including Spain, France, England and Germany, playing competitive league fixtures against the highest-ranked nations in Concacaf such as Mexico, the United States and Canada.

Uefa and Concacaf launched Nations League competitions in 2018, with the confederations staging fixtures in the same international windows, so the mechanics required to set up a joint tournament are already in place.

Under the draft plans the league phase would be played during the existing September, October and November international breaks, followed by knockout matches in March and finals in June.

As the fixtures would take place during international windows that have already been agreed, it is unclear whether the new tournament would need to be ratified by Fifa, although given the world governing body is in the midst of an existential crisis with Infantino facing a leadership challenge that may be a moot point.

With serious discussions having begun only in the last few weeks, the number of teams in each league has yet to be determined, but all 96 members of Uefa and Concacaf would be involved and much of the revenue pooled, generating significant additional income for smaller nations.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino is under pressure with Uefa and Concacaf pushing for his removal and now planning a combined Nations League tournament. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

The commercial appeal of the bigger European teams playing regular competitive matches in North America and Canada would be considerable, while there would also be major benefits for Mexico, whose football federation (FMF) is known to be frustrated by what it sees as the financial limitations of playing within Concacaf.

The FMF has held initial discussions about leaving to join the South American confederation, Conmebol, in a move that would need to be ratified by Fifa, but the prospect of lucrative matches against European opposition could lead to a change of heart.

The proposed new format would replace rather than add to existing international fixtures, while games would be played in geographic blocks to reduce travel.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is also understood to have expressed interest in joining a global Nations League at a future date, and the competition structure being discussed would be flexible enough to accommodate them. The AFC does not currently operate a Nations League, however, so that would be a more long-term aspiration.

Uefa and Concacaf have been working together for some time, and signed a memorandum of understanding to promote greater cooperation at Fifa’s congress in Vancouver in April, but have become even more closely aligned since the World Cup sell-off plan emerged last month.

Both confederations have made it abundantly clear that they regard Infantino’s position as untenable as a result of his role in the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, and are working together to propose an alternative candidate to stand against him in the presidential election next March.

Uefa declined to comment, although one source with knowledge of the proposal confirmed discussions are under way.

Concacaf declined to comment directly, but highlighted the confederation’s longstanding commitment to collaboration, which has led to guest teams participating in the Concacaf Gold Cup.

A historically strong relationship with Conmebol has resulted in many South American teams taking part in the Gold Cup, as have South Africa, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

Sports.title: Manchester United’s midfield rebuild leaves Carrick with no excuses
Sports.content:
Ed Woodward to MUTV in July 2015: “When people see Bastian Schweinsteiger on the teamsheet, that’s going to send some shivers down the spine.” This prediction by Manchester United’s then executive vice-president, about Louis van Gaal’s new midfield signing, proved to be badly off-target as the World Cup-winner’s career at the club proved to be a disappointment.

Two years after Woodward’s bullish statement, Schweinsteiger departed for Chicago Fire with a paltry 35 appearances and two goals for United on his CV, having been forced to train for a while with the youngsters by José Mourinho, Van Gaal’s successor. Here, in microcosm, is the story of virtually all midfield recruits by United for a generation. The hope at the club is that this trend changed this summer, with the arrivals of Youri Tielemans for £35m from Aston Villa and Andrey Santos for £48m plus £2m in add-ons, from Chelsea, with the manager, Michael Carrick, also closing in on Brighton’s Carlos Baleba for a fee in the region of £70m.

You have to go back to Carrick’s own £18m transfer from Tottenham in 2006 for the last elite-level midfielder bought by United, who arrived with his peak years ahead of him and went on to be a consistent force for many years, a strange dereliction of duty for a lineage that boasts Roy Keane, Paul Scholes, Paul Ince, Bryan Robson, Nobby Stiles, alongside other A-list acts.

Since Carrick, Paul Pogba purchased by Mourinho a decade later for a club-record £93.2m possessed the highest ceiling, but the Frenchman was unable to return even seven or eight-out-of-10 displays in most games. Casemiro, who departed Old Trafford in May, came from Real Madrid in 2022 as a five-times Champions League-winner but, at 30, his best years were firmly behind him, and of his four years at United, only the first and last could be rated as high level.

View image in fullscreen Manchester United have been linked with a £70m swoop for the Brighton midfielder Carlos Baleba. Photograph: Jeff Mood/ProSports/Shutterstock

Cite any other signing who has patrolled United’s midfield since Carrick and you are naming mediocrity in a United shirt, at best: Fred, Morgan Schneiderlin, Ander Herrera, Sofyan Amrabat, Daley Blind and Manuel Ugarte among those on that list. The exception is a home-reared player – Kobbie Mainoo. And even a teenager who scored the winner in United’s 2024 FA Cup final triumph against Manchester City and started England’s 2-1 Euro final loss by Spain that summer, was discarded by Ruben Amorim before Carrick’s mid-January appointment, after the Portuguese’s sacking, saved his United career.

So we arrive at the start of a new campaign and Carrick’s move to end this poor engine-room policy reaches Baleba. If the 22-year-old is acquired, he will join Santos, another No 6, and Tielemans, a No 8 who will compete with Mainoo, in a central cadre that has legs, skill, aggression and knowhow. Mason Mount has also shown to be a another viable midfield option during pre-season. The 27-year-old operated with accomplishment as an attacking midfielder before sustaining his latest injury in the draw with Paris Saint-Germain earlier this month.

It is the latest setback for Mount, but Carrick has brushed aside any concerns regarding his robustness. “First of all Mason is a top player – we have seen that he was one of our best players in the first games,” the manager said. “He was outstanding and has picked up a bit of a knock. But there are no dramas. He has missed some football over recent years and he wants to be fit and be in full rhythm and we want to help him. Mason will be back soon.”

United travel to Hull on Saturday before hosting Ipswich a week on Sunday. Games against two newly promoted teams represent a favourable launch to Carrick’s first full campaign in charge, albeit he branded as “ridiculous” the view that it was an easy start. Yet factor in how a trip to Everton is United’s third game before Manchester City arrive at Old Trafford on 13 September and this is undoubtedly a golden chance for United to plant a flag as a potential title contender.

Reviving United amid the chaos of Amorim’s departure and finishing third last year was a fine effort by Carrick. Yet when he took over, the team were already out of both domestic cups and not in Europe. That left 17 games for the then caretaker to navigate. Now Carrick has a full programme of Premier League, Champions League, Carabao Cup and FA Cup fixture before him: a litmus test of his side, as well as of the 45-year-old.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A squad with the requisite depth of quality is beginning to form. If Baleba is added alongside a left-back – Newcastle’s Lewis Hall and Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly remain on the radar – by 1 September, then Carrick will have been bolstered by four new major transfers. There remains question marks regarding the centre-back unit but ultimately the manager can have no excuses.

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick has had a lot to think about this summer. Photograph: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/Shutterstock

Of Hull being an unknown quantity, Carrick said: “That is the beauty of the new season, for teams coming up there tend to be a few changes, that is the challenge playing against them – we are fully aware of that. Mentally and physically we have done a lot of work”. The last comment applies especially to the surgery undertaken to United’s midfield. At 12.30pm on Saturday, at the MKM Stadium, the picture of how good this has been will begin to emerge.

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for as the new season kicks off
Sports.content:
1 Nwaneri out of Arsenal picture

While Myles Lewis-Skelly looks likely to remain at the Emirates, the same can’t be said for Ethan Nwaneri. The 19-year-old was outstanding in his breakthrough season for Arsenal in 2024-25 but barely featured last season and was sent on loan to Marseille. That didn’t really work out and Arsenal are now exploring another temporary move to ensure Nwaneri gets regular football this season. Milan, RB Leipzig, Dortmund and Fulham are all thought to be interested, with Nwaneri unlikely to feature on the bench for Friday’s opener against Coventry as a result. Whether Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus are available remains to be seen as Arsenal attempt to find suitors for the Brazil duo. Ed Aarons

Arsenal v Coventry City, Friday 8pm (all times BST)

2 New United pair down for Tigers test

Manchester United’s summer transfer business has focused on recruiting in central midfield. It will be interesting to see who Michael Carrick selects in two key roles for the first game of the season. Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans have been present for more of pre-season than Kobbie Mainoo, who did not play a minute for England at the World Cup and was a late returner to Carrington after a holiday. Carlos Baleba surely will not have arrived in time to start at Hull. Mainoo is in the best position in the long term but if Carrick decides to ease him into the season, it would be intriguing to see how Santos and Tielemans team up, the stress test for a new partnership that could provide the perfect balance of defensive awareness and ability to move the team up the pitch. Will Unwin

Hull City v Manchester United, Saturday 12.30pm

3 Swapped pair face former clubs

Neither Everton nor Crystal Palace have enjoyed a particularly scintillating summer of transfer activity but combined to make headlines with a swap deal between Dwight McNeil and Brennan Johnson. The pair will face one another – and their former clubs - on the first weekend of the season, eager to prove what their worth to their new teams. McNeil was rarely a regular on Merseyside but had a positive second half to last season, ironically after a move to Crystal Palace fell through at the last minute. Johnson did not settle at Selhurst Park, unable to crack the code that would get him into the starting lineup on a weekly basis, after moving from Spurs. A fresh start should reinvigorate the duo and there is no better way to further boost the mood than beating a former employer. WU

Everton v Crystal Palace, Saturday 3pm

4 Can Ipswich copy Black Cats’ success?

Ipswich clearly learned a lot from what Sunderland did a year ago, as they went out and bought a lot of players. The Black Cats quickly moulded their 19 acquisitions into a successful unit but at least they had the positive of a head coach in Régis Le Bris who had his feet under the table. Gary O’Neil is the new man at Portman Road and he has 12 signings – at time of writing – to potentially use for the opener. The record arrival, Emersonn, who has moved to Portman Road from Toulouse, is the most eye-catching of those who have been acquired. The Brazilian has an underwhelming career goalscoring record and a few question marks hanging over his head. Even though it is their first game, Ipswich need to pick up points at home, and to do so require a striker who can cause problems for defenders. How quickly Emersonn adapts will be critical for the Tractor Boys’ success this year. WU

Ipswich Town v Sunderland, Saturday 3pm

View image in fullscreen Emersonn is one of a number of big-money signings made by promoted Ipswich this summer. Photograph: Keeran Marquis/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

5 Glasner’s tough Diomande ready for debut

August is the season for debuts and no one will be more satisfied than Oliver Glasner when Ousmane Diomande steps over the white line at the City Ground. Glasner wanted the Ivorian centre-back to replace Marc Guéhi at Crystal Palace, six months before the England defender departed for Manchester City. Diomande, a £34m buy from Sporting, is expected to line up in a back three for Nottingham Forest against Leeds, when the Austria midfielder Xaver Schlager, who played for Glasner at Wolfsburg, could also make his Forest bow. Diomande is a quick and physical defender but another aspect of his appeal is his aerial power at set pieces. “They’ve both played Champions League football and they are used to competing for titles,” said Glasner. “They can add this winning mentality.” Ben Fisher

Nottingham Forest v Leeds, Saturday 3pm

6 Serene Senesi can bring calm to Spurs

Cristian Romero has taken his maverick brand of defending to Atlético Madrid, upsetting neutral Premier League watchers. His compatriot Marcos Senesi has arrived to shore up things at the back as Roberto De Zerbi desperately tries to steer Spurs away from a third straight season of battling relegation. The all-action Romero had his qualities as a leader and defender but never felt dependable, which is what most want from a centre-back and captain. Senesi impressed during his time at Bournemouth, rarely making headlines but proving himself a calm presence at the back. The Argentinian is good on the ball and will be more adventurous in possession than his countryman. He is yet to be sent off in three seasons as a Premier League player – Romero was dismissed twice in 2025-26 alone, not to mention a one-match ban and a fine for his behaviour towards a referee. His calmness will improve Spurs. WU

Brentford v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm

7 Villa head south besieged by problems

It is surely not how Unai Emery envisaged the countdown to Aston Villa’s season-opener at Brighton on Sunday – and certainly not as he enjoyed the afterglow from the club’s Europa League triumph over Freiburg in May. The manager has an extraordinary number of problems. Take the midfield where the new signings João Gomes and Johan Manzambi are injury doubts. Note: Amadou Onana is a long-term casualty while Youri Tielemans has been sold. It goes on. Emery is about to lose Ezri Konsa to Arsenal – in a summer where Villa have also sold Morgan Rogers and Lucas Digne. They are trying to move on Emi Martínez, while the future of Ollie Watkins is uncertain, with Al-Hilal circling. For the cherry on top, the rampaging 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo is a fitness concern. Emery’s teamsheet will be very interesting. Will he pitch the new goalkeeper, Zion Suzuki, who only signed on Wednesday, straight in? David Hytner

Brighton v Aston Villa, Sunday 2pm

8 Maresca must win to silence City noise

Is Enzo Maresca already under pressure after Manchester City’s 3-0 schooling by Arsenal in the Community Shield? Maybe not, but if the Italian’s new team go down at home to Bournemouth on Sunday, you do not have to be a soothsayer to picture the scrutiny that will follow. Maresca and City are enduring a difficult transfer window, with Rodri’s departure to Barcelona the headline, a dizzying blow that has to be shaken off. The new Bournemouth coach, Marco Rose, has faced City six times in the Champions League with Leipzig and Mönchengladbach, and is sure to order his visitors to go for the jugular at the Etihad. City are vulnerable but Maresca can remedy this with a win of any sort. This, after all, is the job many felt he was the obvious choice for. Jamie Jackson

Manchester City v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pm

View image in fullscreen Anything but a win for Manchester City at home to Bournemouth will increase scrutiny on Enzo Maresca. Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/EPA

9 King Kev remembered at Newcastle

Kevin Keegan was supposed to have been the guest of honour at St James’ Park on Sunday, but his death from cancer in July means this meeting of two of his old clubs will turn into a tribute to one of English football’s enduring heroes. Keegan’s family will be present to witness an outpouring of love for the former Liverpool and Newcastle forward and (twice) Magpies manager. Once the game kicks off, all eyes will be on Alexander Isak, a St James’ Park old boy whose decision to force a £125m move to Anfield last summer did not go down well on Tyneside. The Sweden striker, making his first return to Newcastle, has much to prove at Liverpool, and now has a new head coach to impress in Andoni Iraola. Newcastle too have a new face in the home dugout, where Matthias Jaissle will occupy the technical area for so long inhabited by Eddie Howe. Louise Taylor

Newcastle v Liverpool, Sunday 4.30pm

10 Former Madrid managers meet in capital

Real Madrid’s two head coaches from last season meet at Craven Cottage, with the focus on Xabi Alonso, rather than Álvaro Arbeloa. The Fulham man, however, may have more to prove in the Premier League. His managerial career has been less prominent than that of his Basque rival – and he has clearly insisted on snapping up talent from the Bernabéu. Gonzalo García and César Palacios have made the trip over from the Spanish capital with Arbeloa. It shows great faith from the former Liverpool defender but it does put extra pressure on the trio, their fates now permanently intertwined. All three need a positive start to show they merit being in the Premier League. Otherwise, it would be very easily to criticise them individually and collectively. WU

Sports.title: Crystal Palace agree Disasi loan and tell Manchester City that Wharton is not for sale
Sports.content:
Crystal Palace have agreed a deal with Chelsea to sign Axel Disasi on loan and are expecting further interest in some of their key players in the final week of the transfer window, having informed Manchester City that Adam Wharton is not for sale.

Palace have been searching for a replacement for Maxence Lacroix after selling the France defender to Chelsea and are also understood to have approached Xabi Alonso’s side over a potential move for Josh Acheampong. But with Chelsea not willing to allow the England Under-21s international to leave Stamford Bridge, Palace have opted to bring in Disasi instead. The 28-year-old, who spent the second half of last season on loan at West Ham, is set to complete his medical on Friday.

Palace are also hoping to bring in a midfielder before the deadline and have expressed an interest in signing Kévin Danois from Auxerre and Monaco’s Lamine Camara. But it is understood the Conference League winners are determined to keep Wharton after City made an inquiry about the England midfielder this week. The 22-year-old has three years left on his contract at Selhurst Park and it is thought Palace would demand a sizeable fee to consider selling him. Liverpool and Chelsea have both also shown interest in Wharton in the past, with the latter said to be monitoring his situation should City make a bid for Enzo Fernández.

Pierre Sage is hoping Wharton will stay for another season. “We sold big players and now I think it’s not the moment to do that,” said Palace’s manager as he prepared for their Premier League opener against Everton on Saturday. “Adam can play at a big club but I think one year with us, one year with a new dynamic, will be good for him and we need him.”

Sage delivered the same message about Ismaïla Sarr after Palace turned down a bid of about £26m from Galatasaray for the Senegal forward. The Turkish side are expected to return with an improved offer and could face competition from their Istanbul rivals Fenerbache for last season’s top scorer. “We will keep him,” said Sage. “He’s a really important player for the club and for us. He will be able to play this weekend.”

There is, however, a strong possibility that Daniel Muñoz could depart after Palace signed Anan Khalaili last week, and given his fellow new recruits Óscar Mingueza and Zavier Gozo can also fill the right-wingback role. The Colombia defender has entered the final two years of his contract and is thought to be valued at about £25m, with Everton, Nottingham Forest and Tottenham having been linked with him in recent days.

Sports.title: Jovial Jakirovic determined to haul Hull over and beyond Coles’ relegation jibes
Sports.content:
On a baking spring bank holiday, Sergej Jakirovic basked in the glory of Hull’s fairytale promotion to the Premier League in an address to 40,000 ecstatic supporters from the balcony of Hull City Hall. “I only had one task before the season – to stay in the Championship … I failed. We’re going to the Premier League!” roared the Jakirovic to the delight of those in attendance.

Oli McBurnie’s late goal had secured a 1-0 win over Middlesbrough in the Championship playoff final 48 hours earlier, clinching one of the unlikeliest ascents for years. Hull only survived relegation to League One on goal difference in 2024-25 but Jakirovic, an intriguing character and fine raconteur, proved the man with the alchemist’s touch.

Three months on from those wild celebrations, the Bosnians new-look side must defy the odds again – and then some – to survive in the Premier League. Hull have been written off as relegation certainties by bookmakers and pundits, including former England duo Carlton Cole and Joe Cole, who ridiculed them on their podcast this week. “Hull are gone, man,” said the latter. “They have spent £70m and I’d be stunned if they stay up. They have come in through the back door, they’ve slipped in.”

Such barbs do not faze Hull’s head coach, who was in typically ebullient mood before Manchester United’s visit to the MKM Stadium on Saturday lunchtime. “I’m buzzing,” said the 49-year-old. “Of course there’s a very big gap between the Championship and Premier League. We’re up against the best teams, players and managers and I’ve seen all the predictions. But it’s a great motivation to prove them wrong because we don’t have anything to lose.

“What we did last season was a very big achievement, but this is football and what happened yesterday doesn’t matter any more. We want to improve and show that we can develop to do even better as a team – and of course we need another miracle to survive. It will be an even bigger achievement than winning promotion if we manage to stay up. We need 40 points, so everything is very clear.”

View image in fullscreen Jens Hjertø-Dahl, one of Hull’s new arrivals, heads at the Nice goal during last Saturday’s pre-season friendly. Photograph: Richard Bierton/Every Second Media/Shutterstock

Jakirovic has made the people of Hull walk a little taller in a city which has received more than its fair – or rather, unfair – share of negative publicity at times. What did he make of the jibes from both Coles, which provoked such a furious backlash from Tigers fans? “It was stupid and disrespectful towards the club and players because we earned everything on the pitch – nobody gave us anything for free,” said Jakirovic. “It’s not fair, especially when it’s coming from ex-players who know how hard players work to reach the Premier League. If they were in my position they would fight, so it’s easy to say we’ll finish 20th, but can they bet on that? They can put everything on that or they can lose, so we will see. But we’re not here by accident.”

The club’s high-profile chairman Acun Ilicali, who has said he will keep faith with Jakirovic even if Hull go down, has made 11 new signings – several of whom are currently injured – and broken the club’s transfer record twice in the process. The recruitment drive, described by some as scattergun, is also not over “We’re expecting three or four more players,” Jakirovic said. “We’ve signed some good players with potential, but I’m also aware that they need more time to adapt and build chemistry with the team.
