“Mr Chairman and I have had a very good connection since our first meeting and we do everything together. In all decisions, we are always speaking and trying to improve our team in many ways.”

Hull’s dramatic rise last season – their fourth promotion to the Premier League from 2008 onwards – caught the imagination, and Jakirovic is a good story in his own right. Born in Mostar in Bosnia and Herzegovina, then part of Yugoslavia, the imposing former centre-half grew up in Metkovic in Croatia. His childhood experiences – running from fighter plane bombings and taking shelter during the 1990s Balkan wars – deeply shaped his resilience and perspective on life.

Jakirovic’s playing career included spells in Slovakia, Slovenia and Bulgaria before he moved into management and eventually landed in Hull – his eighth club in nine years – last summer. “I always sleep like a baby because this is just sport at the end of the day,” he said with a smile. “I have to be fresh on Saturday; I also need to show my potential and prove that I can handle this stage. And I don’t have any doubt because I’ve showed already that I’m capable of doing some great things.”

Sports.title: PSG are the best team in Europe. The rest of Ligue 1 are just trying to survive
Sports.content:
On the eve of a new Ligue 1 season, many clubs seem a little distracted. Even those accustomed to competing at the top have concerns that transcend the pitch. In a league that contains the greatest team on the continent, the focus of the majority of clubs has shifted to surviving and providing, rather than competing.

Any fighting spirit has long since been kicked out of Paris Saint-Germain’s competitors; back-to-back Champions League titles will do that. It feels like a long time ago since Kylian Mbappé moved to Real Madrid on a free transfer, leaving behind a scent of opportunity that filled the nostrils of Marseille, Monaco and Lille. Roberto De Zerbi was bullish when he joined Marseille. “I’m not here to finish second,” said the manager, who has since moved to Tottenham. Finishing second has now become an aspiration, especially for a club such as Marseille, given their predicament.

Of all of the distracted teams, Marseille are the most preoccupied with off-field matters. While the club avoided a European ban, allowing them to compete in the Europa League this season, Uefa’s tone was one of a final warning: redress the financial imbalance or you’re out.

There has been a change in the dugout, with the (almost boringly) dependable Bruno Génésio coming in for Habib Beye, who replaced De Zerbi in February, but the demands made by Uefa – and the DNCG, French football’s financial watchdog – have prevented the club from making a single signing. There have been plenty of sales (Mason Greenwood, Facundo Medina, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang and Gérnoimo Rulli have all left on permanent deals), but not enough for Marseille to contemplate dipping into the market themselves.

Marseille’s “everything must go” sale suggested the club were in survival mode and their reaction to Pierre-Emile Højbjerg refusing a move to Newcastle confirmed it. He was stripped of the captaincy for the club’s friendly against Atlético Madrid. Génésio said it was a decision made above his station and one he disagreed with. “I am an employee. I have to agree to certain obligations,” he said.

View image in fullscreen Pierre-Emile Højbjerg was stripped of the captaincy for Marseille’s friendly against Atlético Madrid. Photograph: Icon Sport/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

Génésio wants to keep Højbjerg, but the austerity cure ensures the club are hell-bent on doing the opposite. It is a situation that perfectly encapsulates the conflict between sporting ambition and financial necessity, familiar to many clubs in Ligue 1, and increasingly those competing towards the top of it – lest we forget Lyon’s recent brush with administration.

With the authorities “supervising their wage bill”, Monaco have made savings this summer. Maghnes Akliouche’s £43m move to PSG has been programmed for some time, and Folarin Balogun and Lamine Camara may still bring in big fees before the end of the window. The unexpected sale of Aladji Bamba to Newcastle for £34m has given the club more breathing room in their quest to cut costs and raise funds.

TV broadcasting rights are no longer the lifeblood of Ligue 1. Instead, French clubs rely on the reckless abandon of Premier League sides making multimillion-pound bets on unproven young players. Bamba had played 18 league games when Newcastle came with the big money. Ligue 1 has always been a ​stopover for its top talents, but the rate of churn has hit new levels. Liverpool did not wait around before signing Jérémy Jacquet and Mamadou Sangaré only needed one campaign at Lens to convince Brentford he was worth an expensive bet.

Even those in stronger financial health cannot resist advances. The prospect of coaching Lens in the Champions League could not prevent Pierre Sage from crossing the Channel to join Crystal Palace. Sangaré made a similar journey, while Adrien Thomasson, Malang Sarr, Allan Saint-Maximin and Wesley Saïd – all instrumental in Lens’ second-place finish and maiden Coupe de France triumph last season – have been lured away. Success can be a poisoned chalice. At least their rebuild, under Dino Toppmöller, looks intelligent. You’d expect nothing less from Lens, but their pillaging once again exposes the limits to success in Ligue 1 for clubs that do not go by the name PSG.

View image in fullscreen Allan Saint-Maximin celebrates after scoring for Lens in the Coupe de France semi-final against Toulouse. He has now moved to MLS. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters

The reigning champions, who are in search of a sixth consecutive league title, have often been accused of being distracted by the Champions League. When you win it two years in a row, you can justify it, but after their close race with Lens last season it isn’t an accusation that can be levelled at them this summer. Their starting XI is already the best in the league and beyond, so PSG’s transfer guru, Luís Campos, has focused on improving the second string that more often than not will be trotted out in Ligue 1.

Ferran Torres, Akliouche and Mika Godts are upgrades on the departing trio of Gonçalo Ramos, Lee Kang-in and Randal Kolo Muani, even if they will struggle to dislodge the current starters in the PSG attack. Lucas Digne is a shrewd pick as back-up to Nuno Mendes, too.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

PSG will probably have an easier ride in the league this season as the teams chasing them have either regressed or stagnated. Rennes, who must this season contend with European football for the first time in three seasons, are the only side that finished in the top seven last season that – on paper – look stronger than they were at the start of the summer.

Wealth immunises Rennes, to a degree, but Strasbourg are weaker after losing important players to Chelsea. Emanuel Emegha, the club captain, has been followed out the door by Valentín Barco, with the goalkeeper Mike Penders returning to his parent club after a loan spell at the Meinau. The latter has been replaced by Filip Jörgensen, who will have to play a “crucial role”, in the words of their new manager, Hugo Oliveira, formerly assistant to Marco Silva at Fulham. Time will tell if Jörgensen is up to the task; he was surplus to requirements at Stamford Bridge so it may be a move born out of convenience. In any case, he will be busy if pre-season is anything to go by; Strasbourg have conceded 21 goals in their seven friendlies.

The managerial upheaval, from Liam Rosenior to Gary O’Neil, and now to Oliveira, also contributes to a feeling of instability at Strasbourg, one of 10 clubs part of a multi-club model in Ligue 1 this season. That, in itself, adds a feeling of “Who is this even for?” to the upcoming season. Not all clubs in these models are subservient, but nor do their own interests always guide decisions.

Rosenior knows all about that. The new Paris FC manager is one of two coaches returning to France in search of redemption following failed stints in England, with the former Southampton head coach Will Still joining Auxerre. There are also some more adventurous appointments, in the form of Davide Ancelotti at Lille and Filipe Luís at Monaco. There have been an incredible 12 managerial changes in France’s top flight for this season: plenty of change, even if some things will almost certainly stay the same.

This is an article by Get French Football News

Sports.title: Arsenal wonderboy Max Dowman, 16, collects his GCSE results and leaves £30,000-per-year school for Premier League stardom
Sports.content:
Premier League record-breaker Max Dowman has collected his GCSE results and is leaving school on the eve of his first season full-time as a professional footballer.

16-year-old Dowman, the Premier League's all-time youngest goalscorer, is pictured in his uniform and wearing braces receiving his results at the £30,000-a-year Brentwood School in Essex yesterday.

Dowman juggled school work with football last season as he broke through at Arsenal, including scoring against Everton at the Emirates Stadium in March to help the Gunners to the title and collecting his winners' medal in May.

He is still too young to even share a dressing room with his senior team-mates under football's safeguarding rules but is expected to play an even bigger role at Arsenal as they defend their title this season.

And Dowman will now dedicate himself to football full-time while many of his school friends move on to Sixth Form and their A-Level studies.

Max Dowman is pictured picking up his GCSE results on the eve of the Premier League season

Dowman, a breakout star for Arsenal last season, will now move into football full-time

'I would like to take this opportunity to say a huge thank you to Brentwood School for everything they have done for me during my time here,' Dowman said yesterday.

'Although my journey at the school is ending earlier than expected as I pursue my football career, I will always be incredibly grateful for the support that the school and the staff have given me.'

Brentwood say nearly 60 per cent of the GCSE grades awarded at their school were 7 to 9, the equivalent of A or A*.

Dowman added: 'The lessons I have learned, both on and off the pitch, will stay with me as I take this next step in my journey. A special thanks to Mrs Crowley, Mr Gamester and Miss Antonello for their kindness, support and encouragement throughout my time at Brentwood.

'I will always be grateful for the difference they have made to my experience here. I leave with some fantastic memories and friendships that I will always cherish. I am excited for what the future holds, but I will always look back on my time at Brentwood with great pride and gratitude.'

Brentwood name Chelsea legend Frank Lampard, writer Douglas Adams, broadcaster Noel Edmonds and actor Griff Rhys Jones among their most famous alumni.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury says Anthony Joshua fight is set to be CALLED OFF because 'money-thirsty piece of s***' Eddie Hearn wants more cash - as he calls out 'drug-dealing idiot' AJ in explosive rant
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury says his long-awaited heavyweight fight with Anthony Joshua now 'doesn't look like it's going to happen' - in a long, explosive rant at his rival and 'money-thirsty' right-hand-man promoter Eddie Hearn.

Joshua and Fury are understood to have signed contracts to fight on November 20 in New York City but Hearn has insisted there is still work to be done on the deal - and the situation has now blown up over the terms.

Fury accused Hearn of 'wanting more money' from Saudi boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh and funding his Saudi-linked snooker, boxing and darts ventures off the back of the prospective Fury-Joshua fight.

In a post on Instagram today, Fury, 38, said: 'Quick update: Doesn't look like they're going to sign the fight, doesn't look like it's going to happen. All because Eddie Hearn and that want more money.

'They've already had that much money off of Turki in the last few years, Eddie and AJ. They've had boxing deals, darts deals, snooker deals, they've had everything. And yet they've had the audacity and cheek of flea-bitten rats to ask for more money from Turki, who's given you everything combined in the last couple of years.

'You're disgusting, money-thirsty pieces of shit. It is what it is, same old cliche a decade later, keep running you little cowards.'

Tyson Fury has suggested his fight against Anthony Joshua is now unlikely to happen

Fury's rant included barbs at promoter Eddie Hearn and 'coward' Joshua

Hearn revealed it was written into 36-year-old Joshua's contract that the fight had to be staged in Britain - only for reports of an agreement to fight at New York's Madison Square Garden to emerge this week.

'All this talk of, "We want the fight in England, we want this, we want that'. It's only to get more money to go to America," Fury added.

'Look at the money he's had off Turki, and yet he still has to do darts deals and snooker deals off the back of my fight. That's got fuck all to do with you, Eddie. You're paid a percentage of Joshua's wages. You're not the promoter, you're not f*** all. You're just a bag carrier like you've always been. End of.'

And he turned more ire on Joshua, who this week was called 'dangerous, reckless and stupid' by boxing legend Johnny Nelson for sharing golf buggy stunts online eight months after surviving a car crash that killed two of his closest friends.

'Tell you what it is, I've never seen such cowardly-a** men in my life,' said Fury. 'You got one sausage up and down on holiday trying to jump off golf buggies. Has he not learned his lesson? He could break his arm, break his leg. Fight's off. Don't even give a f*** about the fight. You pieces of s***. Cowards.'

In a later video, an increasingly exasperated Fury added: 'You 50 pence drug-dealing f***ing idiot. A few muscles don't scare me. Lifting a few weights and doing a couple of CrossFit sessions don't bother me.'

Fury said Joshua had 'not learned his lesson' after a golf buggy video emerged this week

In 2011 Joshua avoided a jail term for possession of cannabis after being found not guilty of attempt to supply.

'I'd drink 20 pints and still beat the f*** out of you,' Fury continued. 'I won't be bothered for you or 50 men like you, that's a f***ing fact. Cause I'm the f***ing Gypsy King, and I'll tear you to pieces, you piece of s***. You and your f***ing full team. Eddie Hearn's a w****r, they're all f***ing scumbags. All scumbags!'

Fury is threatening to fight a different opponent in November if an agreement with Joshua is not reached.

According to IFLTV, Hearn has confirmed that Joshua and his team had requested an increased fight purse to cover the tax costs of the bout taking place in New York.

The promoter is not believed to have received a response to his request for the past three days.

Fury previously announced on Tuesday that the fight was on the verge of being publicised, with the Gypsy King taking to Instagram to share that 'a big fight is on the horizon'.

Fury publicly called out Joshua to make their fight after his win against Arslanbek Makhmudov

But Hearn stressed that there were still elements of the deal to be agreed due to the changed location of the fight, with Wembley preferred by Joshua's camp for the all-British affair.

Speaking in an interview released after Daily Mail Sport's story broke, Hearn added: 'It seems like everyone is adamant the fight takes place in New York. There isn't really any consideration or willingness to speak to the government. Sadiq Khan, Transport for London. It's just like "we want to do this fight in America".

'Tyson Fury has agreed to do it in America and we haven't at the moment. We are talking through a roadmap of what that might look like to change the deal and if they do all the things we've discussed and agreed in principle, then I think there is a very good chance the fight will happen in America.'

Madison Square Garden was the site of one of Joshua's greatest defeats - his shock loss to Andy Ruiz Jr in June 2019.

Talks between Fury and Joshua over their long-awaited showdown have been part of boxing's conversation since 2017, with the biggest opportunity coming in 2021 when the two men appeared to be moving towards a two-fight agreement.

A deal was publicly discussed, but the proposed fight ultimately collapsed after Fury became obligated to face Deontay Wilder following an arbitration ruling.

Fury subsequently fought Wilder for a third time, while Joshua suffered back-to-back defeats against Oleksandr Usyk, losing his WBA, IBF and WBO titles in 2021 before being beaten again in their 2022 rematch.

Sports.title: Premier League's SEVEN big issues: IAN LADYMAN on why Arsenal might be less effective, flawed Liverpool, Newcastle freefall fears - and the two English players who MUST flourish
Sports.content:
Premier League's SEVEN big issues: IAN LADYMAN on why Arsenal might be less effective, flawed Liverpool, Newcastle freefall fears - and the two English players who MUST flourish

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Pep Guardiola may be gone from the Premier League but his shadow remains.

Footage from a new Manchester City documentary has revealed the desperate and unusual lengths the great Catalan went to in a bid to energise and motivate his players over the course of his final two seasons.

Watching a genius struggle for new ideas is painful but insightful. Every manager in the game reaches a stage where old methods fail, players stop hanging on every word and the stresses and strains of the job simply become too much.

Guardiola did a decade at City. Jurgen Klopp did almost nine years at Liverpool. So it's now pertinent to ask how far down the line Mikel Arteta can go with Arsenal.

Now deep into his seventh season at the Emirates, Arteta is already the eighth longest serving manager in Premier League history. This season the pressure to retain last season's Premier League title will be significant and we must hope for the good of the competition that the 44-year-old will find the energy he needs to push on into what should be a bright Arsenal future.

The Premier League needs a strong Arsenal and it needs Arteta. The golden age of English top-flight football is over. City v Liverpool – Guardiola up against Klopp – was thrilling but has left a chasm in its wake.

Footage from Man City's documentary revealed the desperate lengths Pep Guardiola went to in a bid to motivate his players during his final two seasons at the club

The Premier League must hope Mikel Arteta, now in his seventh season in charge of Arsenal, still has the energy to push on into what should be a bright future at the club

Arsenal will defend their title as favourites this season and Arteta has suggested his team may play more expansively. We hope he can make good on that intention.

Last season's Premier League pivot towards more direct play was as startling as it was sudden. Arsenal were in its vanguard and for all that it brought them a much-deserved title, nobody can pretend it was particularly exciting to watch.

All leagues move in cycles in terms of their dominant team and indeed their styles. Last season felt rather fallow in England. The league's enormous wealth should ensure it recovers over time but it needs an example to be set at the top end and if that doesn't come from Arsenal this year then it's hard to feel particularly excited by those who would hope to challenge.

City, Liverpool, Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham. We can write the word 'transition' on a large blanket and throw it over the lot of them.

Aston Villa? The double responsibility of domestic and Champions League football will in all likelihood prove onerous again for Unai Emery's impressive and likeable team. Newcastle, meanwhile, may yet freefall having felt the hammer of the league's spending rules.

So Arteta will lead his champions into action at home to Coventry tonight carrying the pressure that comes with expectation. Hoping to win a title and being expected to are quite different things.

Arteta suggests Arsenal will play more expansively and the league needs the Gunners to set an example in a season when their most likely challengers look to be going through transitions

New guidelines for referees may reduce Arsenal's effectiveness at corners and set pieces

His team's meek defeat by PSG in the Champions League final last May underlined the limitations of Arteta's pragmatic football. This season new guidelines for referees may reduce Arsenal's effectiveness at corners and set pieces.

With all this in mind, Arteta faces the challenge of refitting his plane while flying it. It may take more than a season to successfully transition from one way of playing to another. But it feels as though he must commit to it.

Certainly we must hope the Arsenal manager has the motivation and well of energy and resourcefulness to pull it off.

For if we can't look at Arsenal for hope this season then where do we look?

Can Isak save flawed Liverpool?

Liverpool's fall from grace has been as rapid and complete as any champion team since Leicester a decade ago. Whether they can make up lost ground under Andoni Iraola will depend at least in part on the form of the country's record signing.

The 2025 title winners would appear to have holes everywhere, not least across the back four. Virgil van Dijk, now 35, will be required to carry an enormous load once again.

But it's Alexander Isak who has most questions to answer over the coming nine months. The £125million signing from Newcastle was a disaster last season and if the Swede doesn't bring his best to the table this time, it's hard to see who will score Liverpool's goals.

With Mo Salah gone and Hugo Ekitike facing a long road back following an Achilles rupture, Isak must provide his team with a focal point and a regular supply of goals if this season isn't to go the same way as the last at Anfield.

Isak, who turns 27 next month, had a decent World Cup – with a goal and three assists – and has looked fit during Liverpool's pre-season. He needs to hit the ground running back at his old club on Sunday afternoon.

Alexander Isak needs to step up this season to help a Liverpool side that look to have holes all over the pitch

Palmer and Foden must flourish once more

The truth is that England had a poor World Cup summer. A semi-final appearance may have papered over cracks while Thomas Tuchel's side played Argentina in Atlanta but the fissures were alarmingly big.

What is clear is that England missed the clever, technical and instinctive contributions of players such as Cole Palmer and Phil Foden.

The national team simply cannot afford to go into a home European Championships in two years without such gifted and creative players. So can Palmer and Foden be rehabilitated by new coaches at Chelsea and City respectively?

Palmer is still only 24 and has had injury problems and is about to play for his fourth full-time manager at Stamford Bridge. Foden is a couple of years older and has struggled with some issues away from the field.

We will wait and see if recovery comes but what will it say about our Premier League if two of its most talented academy graduates end up broken and bruised by the environment in which they are asked to play?

England must hopes creative talents like Cole Palmer, pictured, and Phil Foden can be rehabilitated by new managers

Saudis must invest in Newcastle or go

Newcastle's regression represents a huge blow for the watchability and marketability of the English game. The debate over the club's Saudi ownership remains valid and alive but so too is the fact that losing their best players and their manager this summer says everything about how hard it is for upwardly mobile clubs to secure a long-term seat at the top table.

Newcastle flew high under Eddie Howe but ended up with their wings scorched by the sun. Now – with Howe and Anthony Gordon and Bruno Guimaraes all gone – Newcastle's long-term future would appear to depend on their ability and indeed willingness to build a new stadium.

Unless they – and others of their ilk – find ways to make more money, they will never be able to spend more money. The Premier League's spending rules have understandable motives at their core but as we watch clubs like Newcastle crash into the glass ceiling, it's hard to say they have worked.

Newcastle recently had ambitions of winning the Premier League. If they finish in the top eight this season, it will be a surprise.

Will the Saudis stick around? Reasons for doing so are diminishing.

Newcastle's Saudi Arabian owners must demonstrate their willingness to build a new stadium, which looks key for their long-term future. Pictured: Chairman Yasir Al-Rumayyan

Howe will cast a big shadow

Howe's current unemployment may prove a bad thing for Tuchel if his England don't begin their Nations League campaign well when they host World Champions Spain at Wembley next month. Meanwhile the former Newcastle coach also provides Manchester United with a ready-made replacement if things don't go well for Michael Carrick.

United had their hand forced by results under Carrick the caretaker in the second half of last season and as such the former Old Trafford midfielder deserves his crack at the job.

But Carrick must work under expectation this season and also has a Champions League schedule to contend with. It will be very different.

The perfect storm of stumbling rivals and a one-game-a-week schedule that underpinned Carrick's work when he succeeded Ruben Amorim is no more and whether the recruitment of a couple of midfielders and the return from loan of Marcus Rashford has made United's squad fit for purpose is open to question.

Howe ticks just about every box for a club like United while Carrick has an awful lot to prove. He will need some luck.

Eddie Howe's availability could interest England should the Nations League not begin well under Thomas Tuchel

Howe could be viewed as a ready made replacement for Michael Carrick if things don't go well at Man United, with the former midfielder now working under expectation this season

Refs already under pressure

Retiring referee Anthony Taylor has spoken of the pressure placed upon our officials by the media and in particular by former colleagues now employed as TV and podcast analysts.

No mention, though, of the intolerable burden placed on them by the Premier League's ongoing and misguided drive for transparency when it comes to decisions.

Not only do our beleaguered refs have to endure Pro Ref chief Howard Webb poring over their decisions on TV, this season they will see their own explanations behind some calls appearing on the Premier League's website and audio of in-game conversations with players broadcast during televised games.

Remember when the referee's decision was deemed to be final? Not any more and all we can hope as we await an uptick in standards is that new Premier League guidelines are actually enforced.

Less tolerance of holding at corners. A higher bar for VAR intervention. A crackdown on time wasting at restarts and at substitutions.

All have been promised and all are desperately needed.

Will any of it actually happen? It would be unwise to hold breath.

Recently retired referee Anthony Taylor spoke out about the pressure officials are under, highlighting former colleagues discussing decisions on television and on podcasts

Frank Lampard has learned his craft out of the spotlight at Coventry and it is now time to see what he has taken from that as he looks to keep the Sky Blues in the Premier League

Lampard back where he belongs

Nine Premier League clubs will begin the season with new managers – ten if you include Roberto de Zerbi who was parachuted into Tottenham at the back end of last season – and there have been some underwhelming appointments.

Gary O'Neil to Ipswich and Alvaro Arbeloa to Fulham feel particularly unimaginative.

But the return of Frank Lampard to the top flight stage with Coventry feels uplifting and proof that managers can come again after tough times if they are prepared to swallow their pride and work for a while in the shadows.

Lampard said on arriving at Coventry in the lower regions of the Championship in 2024 that he was enjoying time learning his craft out of the spotlight. Now it's time to see exactly what he has taken from that and indeed from hard spells at Chelsea and Everton.

Despite some spending, Lampard's squad still has a top-end Championship look about it and will need some managerial stardust if it's to fight gravity.

The former England midfielder's humility will help him. So may the general lack of quality we tend to see at the bottom end of the top division.

Sports.title: PREMIER LEAGUE PREDICTIONS: Our experts pick which side will win title, who will go down, biggest flop and best new signing ahead of the new season
Sports.content:
It's been a long 12 weeks since the final day of the 2025-26 season but football fans can finally rejoice - the Premier League is back.

With a bang, too. Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea, and Newcastle are just a clutch of the boldfaced names with new managers to keep an eye on, and anticipation is rising to see the summer rebuilds clubs have ushered in.

Now, on the eve of the return of top-flight football, Daily Mail Sport experts Oliver Holt, Ian Herbert, Mike Keegan, Kieran Gill, Lewis Steele, Matt Barlow, Bobby Manzi, and Riath Al-Samarrai make their final predictions.

Tip to win the Premier League

Oliver Holt: Arsenal – they have made two good signings over the summer so far and sold prudently. They have strengthened from a position of strength. They look like a side that will be liberated by the confidence of being champions.

Ian Herbert: Arsenal - crossing the Rubicon to claim the title means so much, removes so much pressure. An excellent transfer window has made them stronger

Arsenal have got the devil off their back by wining their first Premier League title under Mikel Arteta and look stronger than ever

Chelsea welcome Xabi Alonso to Stamford Bridge unburdened by European football and having made key summer signings

Mike Keegan: Chelsea. We saw last season what an absence of European football can do at Manchester United and I like what I have seen at Stamford Bridge this summer given their recruitment pivot. The manager is top class and the old heads they have brought in could be enough for a stunning title assault.

Riath Al-Samarrai: Arsenal. They have the best squad, the least turbulence and have dismantled the mental barriers that previously dominated these conversations. The team to beat.

Kieran Gill: Arsenal. They are more settled than everyone else with Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea going through transitions under new managers. I’m not sure it will even be a close title race.

Lewis Steele: Arsenal. Best team by a distance last season. Manchester City were only close because the Gunners kept on stumbling and keeping them alive. Now, Mikel Arteta’s men will not have the tag of ‘bottlers’ or ‘chokers’ and that will free them up. I’d not be surprised if they won by 10 or more points.

Matt Barlow: Arsenal. Long time since they won back-to-back but strong and stable with main rivals in various degrees of flux. Bruno Guimaraes will improve them. Confident in the knowledge they have what it takes. Free from the anxiety of old.

Bobby Manzi: Arsenal appear stronger than last season, so this will no doubt be proved foolish come the end of the season. But Chelsea have an intelligent manager, have added experience to their squad and no European football to contend with - enabling them to focus on domestic glory. Alonso, against all odds, won the league invincible at Bayer Leverkusen. Chelsea look a good outside bet.

Completing the top four

Oliver Holt: Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea. For different reasons, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak had disappointing seasons with Liverpool last season. Both can flourish this year and Liverpool have new signings to complement them. Chelsea have a first class manager, no European commitments and a more realistic recruitment policy. City have the muscle-memory of previous greatness.

Ian Herbert: Chelsea, Tottenham, Manchester United. Something about Roberto de Zerbi’s energy allied to the big spending makes me think Spurs will be a big story this season. Chelsea on the up, too, but transition time for Manchester City and Liverpool

Mike Keegan: Arsenal will not be far off. You can’t judge City on a Community Shield but, for me, the jury remains firmly out on Enzo Maresca. Liverpool will improve under Andoni Iraola.

Alexander Isak endured a difficult first season at Liverpool but will be a major weapon fully fit

Riath Al-Samarrai: Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea. I don’t envision any of them making a sustained run on Arsenal, but a lot will depend on how quickly Liverpool adapt to Iraola’s style. That’s typically a slow process and a rapid finish. I can see them leading the chase.

Kieran Gill: Chelsea in second, City in third, Liverpool in fourth. Perhaps I’m thinking a tad optimistically on behalf of Xabi Alonso, but he is a good manager who has wielded his influence this summer.

Lewis Steele: Liverpool. People are sleeping on the ability of a much-improved Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz. Their XI is very good but beyond that, it is a worry. Manchester City because they have a deep squad and did not deserve the overreaction or ridicule that came after losing a glorified friendly but losing Pep Guardiola, Bernardo Silva, Rodri and John Stones in the same summer rips their heart out. I’ll go with Chelsea in fourth as I like Xabi Alonso.

Matt Barlow: Chelsea, Liverpool, and Man City. I'm expecting Xabi Alonso to get a tune out of the mass of talent at Chelsea, Liverpool’s big signings from 2025 to improve and City to fade post-Pep Guardiola and post-Rodri but still have lots of quality and Erling Haaland’s goals.

Bobby Manzi: Arsenal, Man United, Man City. Arsenal are nailed on for the top two but will find the first couple of weeks without William Saliba difficult. Manchester United have executed intelligent summer business - they had to improve their midfield and they have. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba are a great blend. As long as Michael Carrick was not a one-hit wonder, they will be up there. A new era at Manchester City but they still have a strong squad to creep into the top four.

The three going down

Oliver Holt: Newcastle almost got sucked into a relegation battle last season. Since then, they’ve lost their biggest asset, Eddie Howe, and their three best players, Anthony Gordon, Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali. Their Saudi owners appear to have disconnected. I like Gary O’Neil, the Ipswich boss, but Ipswich are a classic yo-yo club. And I don’t think Hull have enough to stay up.

Ian Herbert: Fulham, Coventry and Ipswich. Fulham seem a perfect storm: inexperienced new manager, good players have left, an attempt to introduce new system to a club lacking intensity last season. There’s a bond about Hull City. I suspect they’ll be OK.

Newcastle have seen their ranks depleted and a successful manager depart ahead of the start of the season

Mike Keegan: Sunderland, Ipswich Town, Hull City. I’ll probably be the only one predicting Sunderland and I wish I wasn’t because they’re a great club with great fans but they massively overachieved last season and European football this time around could be a killer.

Riath Al-Samarrai: Hull, Ipswich, Fulham. That’s putting a certain amount of faith in Coventry, but Fulham have lost a strong manager and their best player in Harry Wilson. I think they’ll struggle.

Kieran Gill: Ipswich, Hull, Sunderland. I have a hunch that Coventry under Frank Lampard will surprise us, while Sunderland may struggle juggling European football with everything else.

Lewis Steele: Going to be boring and say the three promoted teams. I do think Sunderland will struggle from a bit of second-season syndrome but I think they have just enough quality with Enzo Le Fee, Granit Xhaka, Brian Brobbey et al.

Matt Barlow: Ipswich, Hull, Coventry. Those coming up can all take inspiration from last season’s survivors and there some established teams should be worried by the radical summer of change including Newcastle, Fulham and Palace but the gap still yawns.

Bobby Manzi: Coventry, Hull, Ipswich. Quite simply, the promoted sides are not better than any of the other 17 sides. Coventry have the best chance of staying up but they are lacking in defence.

The biggest overachievers will be

Oliver Holt: Spurs – they have bought well in the summer and in Roberto de Zerbi, they have one of the best managers of this generation. Like Chelsea, they have no European football to drain their resources. They’ll put their recent struggles behind them in style although they could do with a new striker.

Ian Herbert: Everton - drab end to last season obscured the way that David Moyes, such a fine and still underrated manager, has rescued them from annual purgatory. Some good recruits this summer. Moyes buys well. Europe calls.

Mike Keegan: Chelsea, followed by Coventry, who I think will defy the odds and stay up.

Riath Al-Samarrai: Brentford. Again. A smart club with a smart plan and they haven’t been raided quite like Brighton, who would be my second choice if they didn’t have to content with European commitments.

Kieran Gill: I may have hinted at this in my previous answer, but I’ll plump for Coventry. I’m not saying they will suddenly secure Europe. That’s a stretch. Somewhere towards the midtable would be cool.

Lewis Steele: A Brighton or Bournemouth could really flourish but may be held back by Europe. After finishing 17th twice in a row, lowly relegation fodder Spurs might climb up the table…

Tottenham have recruited intensely over the summer, luring Sandro Tonali from Newcastle in a bid to avoid a third 17th-place finish in three seasons

Matt Barlow: Leeds - finished last season at a gallop and reinforced in the summer market. Three winnable home fixtures to start at fortress Elland Road can build a platform for a strong season as others from mid table tackle complications of Europe

Bobby Manzi: Brentford. They were so close to Europe last season - missing out on goal difference. Many tipped them to go down under Keith Andrews and they defied expectation. This season, they may just get Europe. With Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Brighton all playing on Thursday nights, the teams in the middle of the pack could suffer a drop-off in the league. Brentford have kept the majority of their squad from last season together and added sprinkles of quality such as Mamadou Sangare in midfield. They appear well positioned.

The biggest underachievers will be…

Oliver Holt: Manchester City – I know I’ve got City down to finish in my top four but I don’t think they’ll challenge for the title. It’s always tough when a great manager leaves a club after a long time in charge and I don’t think it will be any different for City. It’s a huge test for Enzo Maresca.

Ian Herbert: Newcastle – car crash summer from a club the Saudis couldn’t be bothered to administer properly, now led by a managerial novice. You’re well out of it, Eddie.

Mike Keegan: Manchester United. There is time left in the transfer window for United to strengthen but, as things stand, I do not think they have made the additions which will deliver another Champions League finish.

Riath Al-Samarrai: A three-way tie between Manchester United (thin squad), Newcastle (decimated squad and technical area) and Aston Villa (great expectations after last season but a pretty horrible summer of departures).

Kieran Gill: Aston Villa. As good of a manager as Unai Emery is, Villa have sold some big names this summer, from Morgan Rogers to Lucas Digne to Youri Tielemens, so I’m concerned they may struggle.

Aston Villa have seen their squad stripped of a number of key talents and have European tests to come later in the season

Lewis Steele: Newcastle. The bubble has burst. I did think it was probably right for Eddie Howe to move on but losing Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon in the same window stinks.

Matt Barlow: Aston Villa. Challenging season ahead for Unai Emery. Lost Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne. Ezri Konsa leaving. Emi Martinez and Ollie Watkins unsettled. Key staff gone, too. And has a Champions League campaign to plot.

Bobby Manzi: Bourmemouth. It’s only natural to have a comedown after last season, finishing sixth on 57 points and securing Europa League football for the first time. Much like with Palace last season, playing Thursday-Sunday will take its toll domestically. A bottom-half finish but a strong European return for the Cherries.

Player of the season

Oliver Holt: There are early signs that Arsenal may have cast off the nerves that afflicted them last season. If they play with more freedom and justify their tag as favourites, Bukayo Saka may rediscover his best form.

Ian Herbert: Declan Rice was the orchestrator and architect of so much about Arsenal last season. I can see him running a side that’s feeling mentally released and free.

Mike Keegan: Cole Palmer. A summer off is incredibly rare in this world of saturated football and the mysteriously-omitted England winger will have a barnstormer.

Riath Al-Samarrai: Easy answer would be Haaland, again, but I’ll go with Odegaard at Arsenal. He looks fit and sharp again, which wasn’t always the case last season, but it’ll be interesting to see how Arteta constructs the puzzle with Rice and Guimaraes (who might well be the star turn – the guy can do everything).

Cole Palmer has had a summer off after an injury-stricken season and should be raring to go

Kieran Gill: Joao Pedro. Just because of what I’ve seen of him in Chelsea’s handful of pre-season games. He’s looking like a superstar, and it is understood he is set to sign a new contract.

Lewis Steele: Since I cover Liverpool I will keep my regular readers happy by going with Isak. I’ll look silly when he does his hamstring on Sunday.

Matt Barlow: Alexander Isak. Back to full fitness after his awful first season at Liverpool and sure to enjoy Andoni Iraola’s full throttle style.

Bobby Manzi: Erling Haaland. Goals, goals, goals. At the World Cup, Haaland proved he can find the back of the net regardless of who is around him - scoring seven in five matches. He’s a machine. Nobody will get close to him.

Signing of the summer (so far)

Oliver Holt: Jordan Henderson – not just because he still retains much of the quality he had in his prime but because he is a symbol of a change in approach that Chelsea desperately needed. Xabi Alonso has some brilliant young players at his disposal but it has to be leavened with experience and Henderson and Danny Welbeck are fine professionals who will provide that.

Ian Herbert: Bruno Guimaraes will look even classier in a world class midfield and his presence will free up Rice. Some tandem they’ll be. The £75m salary may come to look excellent value.

Mike Keegan: Youri Tielemans. For the first time in a long time, Manchester United have signed a player who looks like a Manchester United player. I think he’ll settle quickly at Old Trafford and a much-needed all-round presence in midfield.

Riath Al-Samarrai: Harry Wilson to Leeds for nothing.

Kieran Gill: Arsenal’s £75m landing of Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle. He should fit into that midfield beside Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard nicely.

Bruno Guimaraes represents a coup for Arsenal's recruitment after his move from Newcastle

Lewis Steele: I like some of the low-key ones like Joao Gomes to Aston Villa and Ousmane Diomande to Nottingham Forest and Antonio Silva to Bournemouth. But for the sake of picking one I’ll go Matheus Fernandes.

Matt Barlow: Maxence Lacroix. Should bring much needed leadership and maturity to the heart of Chelsea’s young team and not bad value in today’s world of head-spinning fees.

Bobby Manzi: Youri Tielemans. Manchester United have been gradually improving their squad to mount a title charge by 2028. Last season they bought a new forward line; this season it is the midfield. £35million for one of the best midfielders in the league who is in his peak is the best pound-for-pound signing of a window where midfielders are moving for £100m-plus. Technical Tielemans will give United control of games from deep alongside contributing goals and assists.

The signing I'm not sure about is…

Oliver Holt: It hasn’t happened yet but if it does, I think Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City would be a mistake that would upset the balance and the ethos of the club.

Ian Herbert: Andrey Santos. A curious and very substantial £50m layout on a player who doesn’t really seem to have proved himself as a stellar talent at Chelsea. Odd summer for United.

Mike Keegan: James Trafford. I like Trafford. He’s down-to-earth, a character and clearly a talented shot-stopper. However, in this era of set-piece coaches and goals from corners, I do wonder if he has the physical presence to ensure he lives up to his £40m fee.

Riath Al-Samarrai: Sandro Tonali at Tottenham. The price tag is astronomical.

Kieran Gill: Alejandro Garnacho. Aston Villa have taken a chance on him with a loan – and a conditional obligation to buy – and he has a ton to prove.

Alejandro Garnacho remains a risky deal for Aston Villa after his uneven season in west London

Lewis Steele: Carlos Baleba to Manchester United if it happens. Brighton fans don’t seem bothered about him leaving.

Matt Barlow: Elliot Anderson. Quality player but a huge fee brings great expectation and a difficult time to join Manchester City at the end of an era.

Bobby Manzi: Luka Vuskovic. A teenage defender with a very high ceiling but £50m is a significant outlay for a centre-back who hasn’t played in the Premier League and still has plenty of development ahead of him. He will make mistakes this season - he’s young. Brighton just have to hope he fulfils his potential and eventually reaches his projected future sell-on value. After all, their model is based on calculated risks.

Manager with the most to prove

Oliver Holt: It has to be Enzo Maresca. Following Pep Guardiola is the toughest task in world football and that is Maresca’s fate. Far from universally popular at Leicester City, he left Chelsea in difficult circumstances. I’m not sure he has the personality or the people skills to lead a club of City’s size. If he does, he will join the elite of world coaching.

Ian Herbert: Enzo Maresca. The expectation will be that the prophet of Pep will simply pick up his reins, but history, his own temperament and the Community Shield tell us otherwise. Spectre of those 115 Premier League charges still a shadow on the wall.

Mike Keegan: Xabi Alonso. He got the big gig and, to say it didn’t go well, would appear to be a significant understatement. Arrives at Stamford Bridge with a big point to prove post-Real Madrid, and I think he will do just that.

Enzo Maresca is stepping into enormous shoes at the Etihad as he replaces his former boss Pep Guardiola at Man City

Riath Al-Samarrai: Enzo Maresca at Manchester City, obviously. Seemed a little too pleased with some half-decent work at Chelsea and those shoes he is filling at City are huge.

Kieran Gill: Enzo Maresca. Following Pep Guardiola is no easy task, but Manchester City paid Chelsea a total of £17m to hire him. That brings immediate pressure at a club used to winning.

Lewis Steele: Enzo Maresca. Everyone is out to get him as we saw with the vultures descending on a glorified friendly defeat against the best team in the country. He has a lot of doubters to silence. Same goes for Andoni Iraola, Xabi Alonso, the list goes on…

Matt Barlow: Enzo Maresca. Just the 15 major trophies in 10 years for Pep Guardiola, follow that.

Bobby Manzi: Alvaro Arbeloa. Arbeloa is a bit of an unknown quantity. Interim at Real Madrid for five months at the end of last season, having previously held youth roles, this is his first genuine crack at senior management. His record at Real was okay with a 64.29 per cent win rate, losing eight games. That would be more than acceptable at Fulham, not so much at Real. But he was credited for how he lifted the dressing room after a tough spell under Alonso. Fulham have enjoyed stability in recent years under Marco Silva: Arbeloa must show he can provide that.

Sports.title: Arsenal complete Ezri Konsa signing: Premier League champions land Aston Villa star in £55m move hours before beginning title defence
Sports.content:
Arsenal have completed the signing of Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa. England defender Konsa, 28, has signed a four-year contract with an option for a further year with the Premier League champions. The 28-year-old had his medical on Thursday ahead of completing his £55m move from Aston Villa - the fee is £51m plus £4m in add-ons. The Gunners' latest signing arrives hours before they begin their title defence against newly-promoted Coventry City at the Emirates Stadium. The fee is a triumph for Villa as Arsenal initially valued the 28-year-old, who had two years remaining on his contract, at £30m. He was not part of Unai Emery's squad for the UEFA Super Cup defeat to Paris Saint-Germain last week as he was away on holiday after the World Cup. Arsenal have signed Aston Villa defender Ezri Konsa in a £51million deal

Your browser does not support iframes.

Konsa featured 48 times last term in all competitions, scoring two goals and contributing one assist, as Unai Emery's side lifted the Europa League and finished fourth in the Premier League to secure Champions League football for 2026-27. He also sported the armband in John McGinn's absence as Villa's vice captain. Konsa played in every game of England's World Cup run as the country finished third. Konsa started seven of the Three Lions' eight matches at the tournament, with Thomas Tuchel largely partnering him with Marc Guehi at the heart of the defence. He also filled in at right back during England's quarter-final victory over Norway.

Sports.title: Tottenham set to shatter £300m summer transfer spend after agreeing £85m deal with Manchester City for Savinho - and MORE arrivals are expected before window slams shut
Sports.content:
Tottenham have agreed a deal worth £85million for Manchester City winger Savinho. The fee is £75m plus a further £10m in potential add-ons, a record sale for City. Savinho's arrival will push Spurs' spending this summer past £300m, although they have recouped about £140m through the sales of Cristian Romero, Djed Spence and Luka Vuskovic. They plan to spend even further however as talks continue over the purchase of Omar Marmoush from City and Liverpool's Cody Gakpo is among their other targets. Daily Mail Sport first revealed Spurs' bid to sign Savinho on May 25 and the Brazilian agreed to the move early on but City's valuation is understood to have fluctuated owing to the inflated prices in the market. They have also been working to add a replacement with Allan Elias of Palmeiras now in their sights. Tottenham have secured a £75m deal plus £10m add-ons for Manchester City star Savinho Daily Mail Sport first reported Spurs' rekindled interest in the winger in late May of this year

Savinho, 22, will have a medical before signing a long-term contract. The Brazilian's move has been over 12 months in the making, with Spurs first attempting to sign him last summer. After finishing a second-consecutive season 17th in the Premier League, Tottenham have recruited bullishly this summer in a bid to stop the rot. Spurs have spent £185m on bolstering their midfield with the eye-catching signings of Sandro Tonali from Newcastle, and West Ham's Matheus Fernandes, with the club's business not yet finished.

Sports.title: New Premier League 2026-27 rules revealed: MORE VAR involvement, strictly timed substitutions - and the plan to crack down on time-wasting goalkeepers
Sports.content:
New Premier League 2026-27 rules revealed: MORE VAR involvement, strictly timed substitutions - and the plan to crack down on time-wasting goalkeepers

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Football officiating seems to be the hardest job in the game these days. It was, and is, never easy, as you will invariably upset at least one set of fans and players while holding the whistle.

Yet, in recent years, with uncertainty amongst supporters and clubs over the intricacies of the rules – and of course the introduction of VAR – it seems as if the job has become impossible.

Now, in the wake of the 2026 World Cup, the Professional Referee Group (Pro Ref – formerly PGMOL) has drawn up almost an entirely new set of rules to be implemented for the upcoming season for officials and fans to contend with.

Here, Daily Mail Sport examines the major changes ahead of the 2026-27 season coming into play from the start of Arsenal's curtain-raiser against Coventry...

New rules for the 2026-27 Premier League campaign

Goal-kick and throw-in countdowns

Since the beginning of last season's campaign, Premier League teams have seen a countdown implemented for goal-kicks to prevent timewasting and intentional provocation of the opponent. From this season onwards, this countdown rule will apply to throw-ins as well.

The refereeing body has made it clear that every goal-kick and throw-in will have exactly five seconds to be taken or the opposing team will receive a corner, or the throw-in will be turned over. This change ostensibly seems positive but may simply result in more controversy if not applied properly and consistently.

The Professional Referee Group (Pro Ref) have introduced a raft of new rules for 2026-27

More VAR involvement

The prospect of a lower threshold for the use of VAR in the Premier League may frighten a few people, but in fact this will likely end up being a very popular change, if executed correctly.

Since the introduction of VAR in 2019, the system was reserved for red cards, penalties and decisions leading to goals such as offsides and fouls. However, inspired by this summer's World Cup, Stockley Park’s help will now be in use for second yellow cards as well – a change that feels overdue.

VAR will also be taking a closer look at set-piece antics such as grappling and blocking, no doubt inspired by the controversy surrounding the number of goals scored from players flooding the six-yard box at corners and free kicks.

Extended time off the field for injured players

For years, we have seen players seemingly penalised for on-field injuries with a 30-second absence from the pitch after getting checked and being given the all-clear from their physios. But with suspicions that players are sometimes faking these injuries to waste time and disrupt the momentum of the game, Pro Ref will attempt to crack down on play-acting by extending the time penalty to one minute.

This could be a seismic change: with the surgical approach of so many modern coaches, being at a numerical disadvantage for up to a minute might prove catastrophic. But as with all these rules, we shall have to wait and see if they really do have the desired effect.

Timed substitutions

Again, this is another augmentation of an existing rule, with the aim of reducing time-wasting. For the last few seasons, players have been forced to leave the pitch at the closest possible exit point when substituted, rather than leisurely strolling over to the fourth official.

This rule will now be harsher on players, as they will have exactly 10 seconds to reach their exit point. If they fail to do so, the substitution will be delayed by a minimum of a minute and may be much longer at times, as they will have to wait for the next break in play. This means if a player fails to adhere to this new rule, their side could be a man down for some time.

The new rule has been specifically designed so players have no way round it, and surely now we might see the end of subs being made simply to waste time.

Handballs and pass-backs

This one is not so much a new rule but a statement of clarity from Pro Ref after some confusing and controversial moments from previous seasons.

With virtually every Premier League team employing short goal-kicks as opposed to an old-school punt up the field, we often see two centre halves stood either side of the goalkeeper in their own box. This has at times resulted in defenders picking up the ball, or accidentally performing a pass-back as it has been unclear if the ball is in play. In 2024, Arsenal’s Gabriel found himself in this situation in Champions League action against Bayern Munich, and narrowly escaped receiving a red card.

However, from next season onward an act like his will be punished. PGMOL have stated that as soon as the ball returns to the pitch and is distributed by the goalkeeper in any way play has resumed.

Tactical goalkeeper timeouts

Perhaps the most controversial change for the new season is a big one. In a meaningful trial this term, if the game is stopped for specifically a goalkeeper injury concern, the manager must immediately nominate an outfield player to leave the pitch.

Crucially, whichever player is selected must stay off the pitch for a minimum of one minute after the restart of play. Pro Ref has stated that the trial ‘is designed to address occasions where goalkeeper injuries have been used to disrupt momentum, slow the game down or create opportunities for tactical instruction.’

Gianluigi Donnarumma came under fire from Leeds manager Daniel Farke last season as he was accused to feigning injury to 'bend the rules'

Premier League fans will have found themselves increasingly frustrated by these ‘goalkeeper timeouts’ being used as an efficient form of gamesmanship in recent years, so this rule will have a very noticeable effect on players and managers.

And rules the Premier League has chosen to swerve...

Pro Ref have adopted some new rules that were implemented for the 2026 World Cup but not all of them. Some of the key omissions include:

VAR being used to review incorrectly awarded corners: While the top flight will give VAR a greater usage for fouls and second yellow cards, the scope is not extending to corners.

Red cards being given out for players covering their mouths: A contentious decision made by Pro Ref here. Due to the concerning amount of abuse players can give each other in the modern game, many footballing governing bodies seemed in favour of this rule to eradicate covert insults. One of the standout officiating moments of this summer's World Cup involved Miguel Almiron receiving the first red card for the gesture in Paraguay's colours. However, the Premier League believe that their current three-step discrimination protocol is sufficient.

Hydration breaks: Surely a universally agreed-upon positive decision.

'Mistaken identity'/yellows being reserved for diving: A more convoluted but still important clarification, as per International Football Association Board's ruling. A first yellow card can only be reviewed if the card is given to the wrong player, but the decision itself cannot be changed.

Sports.title: Curtis Jones sale means Liverpool have lost 'Scouse heartbeat' for first time in 134 years - here's why it's happened, why the timing couldn't be worse and how Everton have played a part
Sports.content:
There was a heart-deadening moment last season for the player whom Steven Gerrard once declared could become the ‘Scouse heartbeat’ of the Liverpool team.

Curtis Jones had just put in a strong performance in the fourth round of the FA Cup against Brighton, ghosting in to score a technically excellent goal, and you could see from the look in his eyes what it meant to him. Then Arne Slot was asked about Jones’ future prospects in the post-match press conference and warned that he was up against ‘many good players’ in the squad.

It still looked as if the Toxteth-born player had a mountain to climb.

So Jones is going to Inter Milan, bringing the curtain down on 134 consecutive years of the club always having at least one Liverpool-born player in the first-team squad.

The 25-year-old said six years ago that it would be ‘unbelievable’ if the Kop’s chant about a player being ‘the Scouser in our team’ – sung for Trent Alexander-Arnold – were ever directed at him. It won’t happen now. He also reflected that it was ‘important’ for the squad to have a ‘Scouse heartbeat’. There is not one, now.

This unbroken Scouse bloodline extends back through the careers of Gerrard, Jamie Carragher, Robbie Fowler and Steve McManaman in contemporary times. In the great Bob Paisley era, there was Phil Thompson and Sammy Lee, to name just two.

Curtis Jones is joining Inter Milan, bringing the curtain down on 134 consecutive years of the Reds always having at least one Liverpool-born player in the first team squad

Jones, 25, was born in Toxteth and has been with Liverpool since he was a kid

The legendary Bill Shankly had Ian Callaghan, Chris Lawler and Gerry Byrne and many more. Ian St John, one of Shankly’s lieutenants and captains, once said that Shankly’s team-building philosophy was built on a core mix of ‘Scousers and Jocks’.

Don’t let it be said that either of those two great managers would have contemplated, for one moment, fielding a Scouser whom they deemed fractionally less likely to secure a win for them than someone else.

Paisley was brutal in the way he replaced Thompson with Graeme Souness as captain after a poor run of results around Christmas 1981. Shankly and Paisley made it a meritocracy because a deep and visceral hatred of losing was seared across their souls.

Those who later stepped into their shoes perhaps saw the symbolism and good optics of Liverpool-born players even more. Brendan Rodgers described hearing Shankly talking about their value on the tapes of the great man speaking which he played in his car. Jurgen Klopp said he would love a ‘team of Scousers’ and eulogised about ‘Scouse soul’.

But the club’s Kirkby academy simply hasn’t been able to maintain the supply of local players in a development system which, like every other, has an increasingly international dimension.

This is not a new development and to some degree it's cyclical. Carragher discussed the lack of local players following himself and Gerrard through in an interview 21 years ago and there have been some poignant landmarks. Liverpool fielded a player born in the Liverpool region in every Merseyside derby since 1986 – 69 consecutive meetings – until the 2015 fixture.

With players now scouted from across the planet, it is easier to lose those locals who don’t present the promise at the age of 11 which is evident at the age of 18. Anthony Gordon, who was born in Liverpool and a boyhood Red, spent time on the club’s books before Everton snapped him up at the age of 11.

Jamie Carragher and his fellow Scouser Steven Gerrard lift the Champions League trophy for Liverpool in 2005 in Istanbul. But the club will have no homegrown players this season

Trent Alexander-Arnold is another local lad who has left the club in recent years

Everton have been better recruiters of local talent down the decades, arguably helped in more recent years by less pressure and less global scrutiny.

Gordon was back on Liverpool’s radar when Newcastle were ready to sell him, two years ago, as they attempted to comply with PSR. Jarell Quansah was part of a package discussed but Liverpool, who have since sold the centre-half to Bayer Leverkusen, did not want to lose him at that time. How they could have used his presence now.

Managers have craved having a Scouser in the team because they know the value of an individual who can articulate to team-mates, with real authenticity, the expectation, the derby, the history, the peculiarities of the support and the intensity with which the club is scrutinised. A Liverpool-born player requires no explanation.

As one fan posted on social media about Jones' departure: 'Best way to kill a club's identity is to sell all homegrown players for pennies and overspend on unproven foreign players. So stupid.'

Carragher always insisted that Djibril Cisse exaggerated a story of Gerrard using the city as a source of inspiration at half-time during the 2005 Champions League final in Istanbul, but the captain would certainly have spoken from the heart more than anyone on that monumental night.

The timing of this break with history is also unfortunate. Jones leaves at precisely the time that Liverpool seem that much further removed from their roots, with the sale of a third of the club to an investor consortium headed by Jeff Bezos.

Former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp said he would love a ‘team of Scousers’ and eulogised about ‘Scouse soul’

Anthony Gordon, who was born in Liverpool and a boyhood Red, spent time on the club’s books before Everton snapped him up at the age of 11. He has now moved on to Barcelona

American ownership these past 16 years has seemed a little closer to home than it might, given that FSG is based in Boston, Massachusetts, a city with distinct Irish and Liverpool links. Many Liverpool-based supporters feel the consortium’s introduction takes the club that little bit further from them.

There is always an emotional dimension when it comes to city of Liverpool and its football. It’s precisely why Shankly said that the game transcended considerations of life and death. So this is unmistakably a sad day for the place.

Carragher, just like the great men who have managed his beloved club, craves titles and trophies above anything, but it was he who has captured the value of Scousers in the team better than anyone.

‘They will have more of an emotional attachment,’ he said in an interview some years back. ‘It’ll hurt them more when they lose. When they’re playing, they’ll want it more. It’s only small margins, but local players would be more loyal to the club.’

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
