World.title: Uzbekistan, Tajikistan expand scientific cooperation in cotton farming
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Uzbekistan and Tajikistan are expanding scientific and practical cooperation in the field of cotton cultivation, focusing on the assessment of cotton fields, increasing crop yields, and accelerating crop maturation.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbek Ministry of Agriculture, following the delegation’s visit to Tajikistan on August 18–19, which included experts from the Uzbek Research Institute of Cotton Breeding, Seed Production, and Agricultural Technologies.

According to the Ministry, the experts assessed cotton fields in the Bobojon Gafurov district of Sughd region, examining crop conditions directly in the field and developing practical recommendations to improve plant development, increase yields and accelerate cotton ripening.

Cotton is being cultivated on a 25-hectare plot in the area using the “Xinjiang” cultivation method. The crops were planted using a double-row system with a 76-by-10 centimeter spacing scheme.

The fields are also equipped with a drip irrigation system provided free of charge by Uzbekistan’s Bukhara Agrocluster.

Particular attention during the field assessment was given to accelerating and ensuring uniform cotton maturation.

In line with recommendations from Uzbekistan’s Agriculture Ministry, specialists provided practical guidance on the use of ethephon and the effectiveness of a three-stage set of agricultural practices designed to promote earlier cotton maturation.

“Timely implementation of agricultural measures in accordance with established schedules and application rates is essential for healthy and rapid cotton development and for improving yields,” the specialists noted.

The Uzbek experts assessed individual agricultural processes directly in the fields and provided scientific and practical recommendations aimed at increasing productivity and improving cotton quality.

The cooperation is expected to support the introduction of advanced agricultural technologies in Tajikistan’s cotton sector while expanding the exchange of scientific and practical expertise between the two countries.

The joint work also provides an opportunity to test cultivation practices under local conditions and adapt recommendations to the specific needs of cotton growers in Tajikistan.

World.title: Azerbaijan announces new support mechanisms for entrepreneurs
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Economy of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Azerbaijan has announced new state support measures for businesses, including compensation for export transportation and customs clearance costs, loan interest subsidies and state guarantees, according to the Ministry of Economy.

The Economy Ministry said the measures were presented during a meeting between Deputy Economy Minister Azer Bayramov and entrepreneurs operating in the Lankaran-Astara economic region in the city of Masalli.

The meeting highlighted that, in line with the economic policy pursued under President Ilham Aliyev, the government is expanding state support measures and introducing new mechanisms to promote investment and production and increase economic activity in the regions.

Entrepreneurs were encouraged to make active use of the favorable business environment and implement new initiatives.

The ministry said more effective use of the Lankaran-Astara economic region's economic potential, particularly through industrial development, expansion of agricultural processing and industrial production, and creation of value-added and export-oriented industries, could contribute significantly to the region's economic development.

A presentation was held on new and expanded state support measures for businesses, as well as opportunities to promote industrial and investment projects.

The government will cover up to 70% of transportation costs incurred when exporting non-oil and non-gas goods of Azerbaijani origin. The amount of support will be determined based on transportation costs and the customs value of the goods, depending on the mode of transport used.

The new mechanism will take effect on September 1 this year and remain in place for 10 years. It is intended to increase the competitiveness of local products in foreign markets, reduce logistics costs and expand export markets.

The government will also cover part of customs clearance costs for exports of non-oil and non-gas products of Azerbaijani origin. Exporters classified as micro, small and medium-sized enterprises will be eligible for the support.

The mechanism will take effect on September 1 this year and remain in force for five years.

A separate mechanism will make loan guarantees and interest subsidies more flexible and efficient, with the aim of expanding entrepreneurs' access to financing and facilitating investment projects.

Entrepreneurs will receive a subsidy equivalent to 50% of loan interest payments. The subsidy will apply throughout Azerbaijan except for Baku and the Absheron district.

The government will provide guarantees covering up to 90% of the principal amount of loans issued in liberated territories and up to 50% of loans issued in other regions, excluding Baku and Absheron.

The measures are expected to boost regional investment, reduce the financial burden on businesses and provide an additional stimulus to the non-oil and gas sector.

From 2027 to 2030, the government will cover 50% of the connection fee paid by entrepreneurs when new industrial and agricultural facilities are connected to the electricity grid.

A commission established to accelerate strategic investment projects and strengthen coordination among government agencies will process major projects through a one-stop-shop system. The new approach is expected to reduce project implementation times by about 30%-40%.

The ministry said the measures would help reduce the financial burden on entrepreneurs, encourage new investment, expand production, stimulate exports and increase economic activity in the regions.

Entrepreneurs operating in the Lankaran-Astara economic region presented their proposals and initiatives at the meeting, and their questions were answered.

Masalli District Executive Authority head Araz Ahmadov said the new state support measures and meetings with entrepreneurs would play an important role in increasing business activity in the region.

As part of the visit, a meeting was also held with residents of the Masalli Industrial District. The delegation reviewed projects being implemented by entrepreneurs and discussed issues of interest to them.

The Masalli Industrial District was established to support industrial and entrepreneurial development in the region, create new production facilities and increase employment.

Covering 10 hectares, the industrial district is considered important for expanding value-added production and increasing the industrial potential of the Lankaran-Astara economic region.

Operating since 2018, the industrial district provides the infrastructure needed by businesses and hosts various production and processing projects, including the manufacture of plastic containers, furniture, construction materials and other products.

World.title: Federal government to fund majority of ACT gun buyback scheme
World.content:
The ACT will introduce a gun buyback scheme similar to the one in NSW, as part of a national push to strengthen Australia's gun laws.

What we do and don't know about guns in Australia Gun control researchers say we have "no idea" how many black market and 3D-printed weapons are out there.

The agreement between the federal and ACT governments comes after a National Cabinet commitment to "eradicate" antisemitism and strengthen gun laws following the Bondi Beach terrorist attack in December last year.

Last week, NSW announced it would be the first state to begin the national buyback scheme, commencing on November 2.

The ACT committed to being part of the scheme after it was announced in the wake of the attack, but until now has remained in negotiation with the federal government over how it would be funded.

The agreement will see the Commonwealth government fund 75 per cent of the buyback and associated administrative costs, and 100 per cent of the firearm destruction costs, with the ACT government funding the rest.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says national gun reform is important to ensure terrorist attacks like the one in Bondi cannot occur again. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement that the scheme was about taking action to keep communities safe.

"National gun reform is an important part of making sure an antisemitic terrorist attack like we saw at Bondi can't happen again," Mr Albanese said.

" I thank the ACT government for their collaboration as we work to take guns off our streets in order to better protect Australians. "

Currently there are about 23,000 firearms in the ACT, and over 7,000 people who hold a firearms licence.

About 14 per cent of those licence holders are expected to be affected by the proposed firearms cap.

No further details have been given about what date the scheme will begin in the territory, or what compensation will be offered per surrendered firearm.

'Some of the strongest firearms laws in the country'

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr acknowledged that the majority of firearms owners were responsible and law-abiding. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

In a statement, ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr said the agreement with the federal government strengthened community safety, and supported effective firearm reforms across jurisdictions.

"Reducing the number of high-risk firearms in circulation is a sensible and practical measure to help keep Canberrans safer," he said.

"Working with the Commonwealth and NSW ensures a more coordinated approach to firearms safety.

" The ACT has some of the strongest firearms laws in the country and this agreement supports our ongoing efforts to further reduce the risk of firearms falling into the wrong hands. "

Mr Barr acknowledged that "the overwhelming majority" of licensed gun owners were responsible and law-abiding citizens.

Along with committing to the national buyback scheme, the ACT has also proposed a change to its gun laws. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"The buyback scheme will provide compensation while helping deliver further community safety outcomes," Mr Barr said.

The agreement also comes after the ACT government proposed new gun laws for the territory in February, which would see licensed gun holders limited to owning five guns.

The Firearms (Public Safety) Amendment Bill 2026 includes exemptions on that cap, allowing up to 10 guns for occupational and sporting purposes.

It would also criminalise the possession of blueprints for 3D-printed guns, prohibit belt-fed firearms, and re-categorise firearm types.

The bill is still before the ACT Legislative Assembly, and is expected to be debated during the assembly's spring sittings.

World.title: Tony Burke breaks silence on ex-ASIO agent's Bondi royal commission testimony
World.content:
A former ASIO agent who wants to give evidence to the Bondi royal commission can do so in open hearings, the Home Affairs minister says, meaning he does not need a visa to travel to Australia.

It is the first time Tony Burke has publicly addressed the man's intent to testify after previously denying his Australian visa request.

The former agent, known as Marcus, wants to give evidence about what he knew of the Bondi gunmen in the years before last December's terror attack.

He spent years infiltrating Islamic extremist groups in western Sydney, working as a paid source for domestic spy agency ASIO before his cover was blown.

Marcus met the Akrams when he infiltrated Sydney's Islamic State network for ASIO. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

Marcus has repeatedly made a case to give evidence from within Australia, due both to the sensitivity of his evidence and the legal protections he gains from being on Australian soil.

The royal commission has previously held classified hearings to ensure it can take evidence on sensitive intelligence information.

Mr Burke told reporters this morning he had been advised any evidence Marcus gives can be heard in public and heard remotely.

"Mike Burgess, the director-general of ASIO, has advised and made clear to the royal commission that any evidence that would come from this particular individual is declassified," he said.

Ex-spy denied visa ahead of Bondi RC The man who previously warned ASIO about the Bondi gunmen will not be able to give sensitive and classified evidence at the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

"He's happy for it to be given in a complete public forum. It could be given over the phone on (Microsoft) Teams. It could be given in any way that the individual wants."

The royal commission has previously reached out to Marcus, it stated it is "eager" to hear his evidence and work out the best means for that to take place.

He is currently living abroad and cannot reach an Australian embassy.

Separately, NSW Police has also reached out to the former agent seeking assistance with its own investigations into last December's shooting.

Marcus has expressed fears for his personal safety while living overseas. He has sought protection and resettlement in Australia in the past.

His first visa application was rejected on the grounds that immigration authorities did not believe he had a genuine intention to leave the country, and his second application remains pending.

Mr Burke said the applications have followed all the normal channels.

"The department has its normal processes in working out whether or not someone qualifies for a visa under the Migration Act, and there hasn't been interference with that process," he said.

"The department looks at the Migration Act, looks at the application, and makes their own decision."

Advocates maintain call for visa

Whistleblower advocates have continued to back Marcus' cause, arguing the safest place for the former agent to give evidence is on Australian soil.

Marcus has previously told the ABC's Four Corners about his interactions with the Bondi gunmen, Sajid and Naveed Akram.

He claims he warned ASIO about the Akrams years before the attack.

ASIO has described the former agent as disgruntled and unreliable, but Marcus has rejected the characterisations.

Gabriel Shipton, from the whistleblower advocacy group the Information Rights Project, said he is in danger abroad.

Tense exchange at royal commission The witness, a Sydney researcher, questioned Israel's right to exist and was quizzed on her views comparing zionism to violent extremism.

"The protections offered by the royal commission do not extend outside Australia," he said.

"Marcus continues to risk his safety and the safety of his family. He is willing to give evidence and again the government is not acknowledging the threats he is under from the associates of the Akrams."

The group has provided support to the former agent as he lives overseas.

Mr Shipton said he should be allowed to give his evidence within Australia.

"The government has left it up to Information Rights to keep one of its ex-employees safe after years of undercover service, and again the minister has shown they are not serious about hearing evidence that contradicts the facts given by the institution in his own ministry."

World.title: 'Bittersweet': Vulnerable moment becomes national prize-winning photo
World.content:
Melbourne artist Nathan Beard has won the $30,000 National Photographic Portrait Prize for a faceless and intimate portrait of his aunty recuperating after a major medical scare.

Beard captured the private moment while visiting the beloved matriarch, Mae Khong, in Thailand earlier this year.

"On this particular trip she had suffered a fall at home and I was the only one in the house with her," he said.

The winning photograph in the 2026 National Photographic Portrait Prize, titled Mae Khong, by Melbourne artist Nathan Beard. (Supplied: Nathan Beard)

" She insisted that evening, even after the shock of the event, to bathe herself, and to do so independently. "

The National Portrait Gallery's Director of Curatorial and Collection, Isobel Parker Philip, said the photograph conveyed fortitude and strength, coupled with fatigue and vulnerability.

"You can't see her face but that doesn't mean you don't have an emotional connection to her," she said.

"You might look at it and see one of your loved ones; you can read the many, many years of her life experiences in the frame."

Mae died in July, meaning she will never know of the prestigious accolade bestowed on her nephew.

"It is bittersweet being recognised for the award because it's sort of a final gift of hers to me," Beard said.

NghỉNghiêm (AttentionAt ease), 2025 by Phuong Nguyen Le, winner of the $3,000 First Time Finalist Award. (Supplied: Phuong Nguyen Le)

The multidisciplinary artist, who draws on his Australian-Thai heritage, said his aunty was an influential figure in fostering his sense of cultural pride and belonging.

"She always struggled with why I would find her such a captivating subject," Beard said.

" She always thought it was silly that someone would think her worthy of that sort of status. "

Alongside the $30,000 prize money, Beard will also receive $20,000 worth of camera equipment.

UNTITLED_ 01 (Series_ What Remains_), by Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud, depicts a Flemington public housing resident packing to leave her home after it was earmarked for demolition. (Supplied: Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud)

Moments of joy, humour, tenderness

The image is among 30 finalists selected in this year's National Photographic Portrait Prize from more than 1,000 entries.

The selection showcases a diverse array of styles and subjects, from moments of joy and humour to poignant and tender snapshots.

Sublim8 by Camille Perry, a finalist in the National Photographic Portrait Prize 2026. (Supplied: Camille Perry)

"It truly is a celebration of portraiture in its most expanded form," Ms Parker Philip said.

Phuong Nguyen Le won the $3,000 First Time Finalist Award for a portrait of his father, taken to mark the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War.

Earlier this week, Melbourne photographer Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud won the $3,000 Art Handlers' Award for his image of a Flemington public housing resident, packing to leave her home after it was earmarked for demolition.

Holding Space by Adam Edwards was a finalist in the National Photographic Portrait Prize 2026. (Supplied: Adam Edwards)

This National Photographic Portrait Prize was launched in 2007 and is open to emerging and established artists.

This year marks the final iteration of the competition in its current format, with a new prize model to be announced by the National Portrait Gallery in 2027.

Hanging alongside the 2026 show is a retrospective exhibition of almost two decades of finalists' work.

A portrait of actor David Howell by Ingvar Kenne was also a finalist. (Supplied: Ingvar Kenne)

It includes some famous faces, such as former prime minister Bob Hawke sipping a milkshake.

"Photography makes up about 57 per cent of our collection," Ms Parker Philip said.

"It's really important to the gallery and we're excited to support more photographers in the future."

World.title: Live: McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies
World.content:
Logan Morris kicked a bag of eight as Brisbane beat Collingwood at the MCG (Getty Images/AFL Photos)

Reigning premiers Brisbane have sealed a top-four berth with a 63-point win over Collingwood, who will sweat over a knee concern to Scott Pendlebury ahead of AFL wildcard round.

Young phenom Logan Morris kicked eight goals as the Lions were a class above all night and claimed a 25.9 (153) to 15.6 (96) win in front of 66,846 fans at the MCG on Friday.

Collingwood coach Craig McRae opted not to rest any stars, despite being locked into a wildcard game, but may wonder whether that was a mistake after Pendlebury (knee bursa) was ruled out in the second quarter.

Brisbane (64 points) sit third and will stay there unless Hawthorn (60) hammer West Coast, with Melbourne (60) too far back on percentage to catch the Lions.

Coach Chris Fagan wasn't impressed as Brisbane, who led by 75 points midway through the final quarter, gave up six straight goals — a costly percentage hit — before steadying.

The team that finishes third will avoid facing minor premiers Fremantle in Perth and instead take on a decimated and embattled Sydney at the SCG.

The Swans are without stars Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, plus Riley Bice and James Jordon, who were suspended for the rest of the season for "breaching club standards".

Those five players are linked to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel on Monday morning.

Brisbane will have next week off before finals.

Collingwood will desperately hope Pendlebury is available for the wildcard match, against either the Western Bulldogs or Carlton.

The 38-year-old went down into Collingwood's rooms in the second quarter and was later ruled out of the game before halftime.

Magpie defender Dan Houston had his left hand looked at late.

Brisbane defender Ty Gallop appears certain to face match review scrutiny for a dangerous tackle on Charlie West — though the Magpie forward played on.

It was Gallop's first game back after a three-game suspension.

Lions veteran Dayne Zorko could also be looked at for catching Jack Crisp high as he attempted to smother a fourth-quarter handball.

Morris was unstoppable in the first half, kicking four goals, and maintained the rage after the main break.

Irishman Conor McKenna kicked four goals, including two stunners.

McKenna smothered the ball then brilliantly toe-poked through a freak goal from a tight angle.

The dazzling effort was followed by an incredible no-look snap from almost 50 metres out, close to the boundary.

Recruit Oscar Allen jagged four goals, Eric Hipwood kicked three, and Lachie Neale (16 clearances, 35 disposals) and Josh Dunkley (27 disposals) shone.

Collingwood's Jordan De Goey (32 disposals, six clearances, two goals) was superb.

Nick Daicos (26 disposals) and Darcy Cameron sat out the end of the game, while Sam Swadling (32 possessions) was excellent, and Angus Anderson and West kicked three goals apiece.

At halftime, Brisbane led by 22 points, with Morris having kicked four goals.

The Lions exploded after the main break and the contest was over by three-quarter time.

World.title: Man accused of defrauding Indigenous community not of 'dishonest mind'
World.content:
Lawyers representing a man accused of defrauding money meant for an Indigenous community say his actions do not show a "dishonest mind" but a "best effort" to account for where the money went.

Ankumuthi traditional owner Larry Joe Woosup has been charged with two counts of fraud to a value of $30,000 or more each. He has pleaded not guilty.

During the trial this week, the District Court in Cairns heard Mr Woosup and another community member arranged a deal with a mining company over the right to mine bauxite on traditional lands a year after a separate deal with the community reached a stalemate.

Mr Woosup then set up trust accounts with two different banks for the Ankumuthi community, where he was the sole trustee.

The jury was told it was an undisputed fact that Mr Woosup then used the overdraft capacity on one account to transfer and withdraw $110,000 and deposited a cheque for $95,000 from the mining company into the other account, which was then also withdrawn.

The requirement for both trusts was for all money to be used for the benefit of the Ankumuthi community, the court was told.

The crown case

Crown prosecutor Christian Peters told the jury Mr Woosup's dishonesty had been set out in "black and white".

Christian Peters (right) has told the court of Mr Woosup's multiple cash withdrawals. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

He said Mr Woosup was well and truly aware of his role as trustee and had been receiving advice every step of the way.

Mr Peters highlighted the various cash withdrawals from the multiple trust accounts, as well as some of the records of expenditure, including the purchase of three cars and numerous accommodation expenses.

Mr Peters also questioned the responses Mr Woosup gave in a questionnaire for federal court proceedings, where he listed a total of $13,000 in a fortnight as "personal expenses" and multiple cash withdrawals, each up to $5,000 in value, as non-specific "Trust bills".

"What bills? What bills was the trust paying?" Mr Peters said.

He also referenced some of Mr Woosup's conduct in the years after the alleged fraud, where other members of the Ankumuthi community confronted him about rumours he had taken money meant for the community.

The trial is expected to conclude with Judge Joshua Treviño KC's final closing statement on Monday. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

In one witness's recollection, Mr Woosup apologised and asked for forgiveness.

"That is an admission by him … that that money was not used for the principal purposes of that trust," Mr Peters said.

Mr Woosup's defence

Mr Woosup's defence barrister, Matt Jackson, told the court that when questions first started to be raised about where trust money was spent, Mr Woosup engaged an accountant and provided bank statements and receipts.

Mr Jackson suggested to the jury that this was a "pretty good effort" to engage with the process and indicated an "honest state of mind".

He said the prosecution had an issue with Mr Woosup's use of cash and said while Mr Peters had asserted the purpose would be to defy tracing, Mr Jackson insisted it was not uncommon for Mr Woosup to pay bills in cash.

Mr Jackson also questioned if the prosecution had truly provided any evidence the money had not gone back to the community.

He said the cars purchased had been used for cultural surveys on country, and that many of the witnesses called who said they had not received any money only became recognised as Native Title holders years after the events.

Larry Joe Woosup has pleaded not guilty to two counts of fraud to a value of $30,000 or more each. (ABC Far North: Holly Richardson)

The jury heard from Mr Jackson that the many errors in Mr Woosup's documentation were evidence of the passage of time, rather than dishonesty.

"This case is not about what the trust means … it's about what Larry Woosup meant," Mr Jackson said.

He said his conduct, including his denials and apologies to members of the Ankumuthi community after the events, was also consistent with the state of mind that he did not do anything wrong.

"People can apologise for a number of different reasons … it doesn't mean they're trying to hide," Mr Jackson said.

Judge Joshua Treviño KC has begun his summing up to the jury and will continue when court resumes on Monday.

World.title: Jury discharged in rape trial of competitive bull rider
World.content:
The jury in the rape trial of competitive bull rider Clay Benjamin Hall has been discharged after failing to reach a verdict on one of two charges in relation to an incident in Warwick in 2021.

After more than eight hours of deliberations the jury unanimously found Mr Hall not guilty of one count of rape but was unable to reach a verdict on a second count related to the same incident.

Justice Philip McCarthy KC discharged the jury today after it failed to reach a unanimous or majority verdict on the remaining charge.

The court was told Mr Hall met the girl, who was in her late teens at the time, on a street in Warwick, about 160 kilometres south-west of Brisbane, in the early hours of October 2021.

Prosecutors alleged Mr Hall, now 26, raped the teenager after she offered to show him a shortcut to the Warwick Showgrounds.

The court heard the teenager had been drinking and had been at a house party with people she did not know before she met Mr Hall.

Clay Benjamin Hall told police in 2023 that he had been given consent by the complainant. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Mr Hall was in Warwick to watch his brother compete at the Warwick Rodeo.

The court heard Mr Hall, who was not competing because of an injury, had also been drinking before walking to a service station to buy food in the early hours of the morning.

A key issue at trial was whether the sexual activity between Mr Hall and the complainant was consensual.

Defence barrister David Jones KC told the jury it was not in dispute that Mr Hall and the complainant had vaginal intercourse but rejected the allegation that anal penetration had occurred.

Jurors were shown a recording of a 2023 police interview in which Mr Hall said he propositioned the teenager and initially received no response but later he claimed was given consent.

The jury was also shown police interviews conducted with the complainant at hospital on the morning of the incident and later that day at a police station.

The complainant gave evidence during the trial and was cross-examined by the defence.

During deliberations jurors asked to view the complainant's recorded interviews again.

After more than eight hours of deliberations, Justice McCarthy gave the jury a majority verdict direction, allowing it to return a verdict if 11 jurors agreed and one disagreed.

But the jury later indicated it was unable to reach a majority verdict.

While discharging the jury, Justice McCarthy thanked jurors for their work.

"Whilst you may have a frustration, you worked very hard. Your endeavour was appreciated and I appreciated the way you took upon your task in this courtroom," he said.

The unresolved charge remains before the court and the matter will return to the Warwick District Court for a callover on September 17.

World.title: Prominent harness racing stable fined over insurance policy failure
World.content:
A prominent Tasmanian harness racing operator has been fined $8,000 for failing to secure adequate insurance, which came to light after employees were injured in a car crash that killed four horses.

Ben Yole Racing Pty Ltd was sentenced in the Launceston Magistrates Court this afternoon, after pleading guilty to failing to maintain a policy of insurance with a licensed insurer, between July 2022 and December 12, 2023.

The issue emerged after a car crash near Sidmouth in January 2023, where four horses were killed, and injured workers later learned they were not covered by workers' compensation insurance.

The company had more than 30 employees at the time.

Five Yole workers, who were aged between 14 and 20 at the time, were in the car at the time of the crash. (Facebook: The Vigilante News)

The prosecution had suggested the fine could have reached $90,500, while defence barrister Damian Sheales had argued a fine of between $1,500 and $2,500 would have been sufficient.

Magistrate Sharon Cure ordered the company to pay $62,168 to the WorkCover Tasmania Board and fined it $8,000 plus $82 in costs.

The driver crashed a vehicle towing a horse float after working for more than 18 hours, a court heard. (ABC News: Jess Moran)

Magistrate Cure made the point that the case had been dragging on for a long time and agreed with a comment from Mr Sheales that "everyone feels exhausted by it".

She said she accepted the company became aware that it did not have adequate insurance and took steps to address it.

She did not believe the breach stemmed from an attempt to gain an advantage over competitors.

While she said she gave some weight to the nature of work and level of risk its employees faced, she said the legislation does not take those factors into account.

The company was granted a stay of 28 days to make arrangements.

Ben Yole Racing faces further charges relating to failing its workplace health and safety duties, failing to report an incident, and failing to preserve an incident site, to which it previously pleaded not guilty.

These matters will return to court later this year.

World.title: Teenage boy charged with alleged murder of 13-year-old girl fronts court
World.content:
A Children's Court judge has said there are reasonable grounds to suggest a teenage boy committed the murder of a 13-year-old Wimmera girl.

The 16-year-old boy fronted a Children's Court of Victoria on Friday by video link from youth prison.

He is accused of murdering Layla Jeffery, whose body was found in bushland on July 9 after being reported missing from Donald, near Horsham, on July 5.

Judge Jack Vandersteen, the president of the children's court, said: "[The accused has] been charged as a single person and therefore as the principal."

He said there were reasonable grounds to believe the accused committed the offence, and that an item believed to have been at the scene of the alleged offending had been found.

Flowers adorn Layla Jeffery's memorial at the Bullocks Head lookout in Donald. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Order for swabs

Judge Vandersteen granted a police application to get a new DNA sample from the accused, after chief crown prosecutor Kristie Churchill KC asked for the boy's previous sample to be destroyed.

The judge informed the teenage defendant that if he did not comply with the mouth swab, police could use reasonable force to obtain it.

"They will ask you to do it yourself and if you don't, they will do it," the judge said.

The accused replied: "Alright."

When asked if he had any questions for the judge, the accused said: "No, your honour."

Slouched, yawning

The accused attended his court appearance wearing a black beanie and a black T-shirt layered over a white long-sleeve top, with Judge Vandersteen asking him to remove the beanie at the start of the hearing.

After doing so, the teenager slouched down with his elbows on his knees for the rest of the hearing — periodically stretching, yawning and looking up at the camera.

The case has been adjourned until September 10.

World.title: The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated
World.content:
PoliticsNSWMedia & marketing The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated August 21, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An investigation that revealed the NRL’s top referee had a gambling problem, photographs capturing the Bondi Beach terror attack, and a profile of Australia’s cardboard king are part of the Herald’s award-winning coverage celebrated at the Kennedy Foundation’s Excellence in Journalism awards. The awards, across 37 total categories, were announced at a ceremony at Sydney’s Royal Randwick Racecourse on Friday night. Edwina Pickles has been recognised for her photographic coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack. Edwina Pickles Senior sports reporter Chris Barrett won the Outstanding Sport Reporting category for an investigation revealing rugby league’s most high-profile referee, Ashley Klein, had a $400,000 gambling problem, which the code knew about for four years while letting him continue to officiate matches at the top level. Photographer Edwina Pickles won the Outstanding News Photography category for her coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack in December.



Deputy state topic editor Michael Ruffles won the Outstanding Three Headlines category. Among his submissions was “The lying, the Ferrari wish and $400,000 in cash in the wardrobe”, which related to chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont’s coverage of former bankrupt Warren Jack’s “fanciful” explanations to a Sydney court during a dispute over unpaid loans. Cartoonist Matt Golding picked up the Outstanding Cartoon award for “Playing Trump”, which depicted Russian President Vladimir Putin passing the dice to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the pair play a board game called “Trump” with North Korea’s Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Cartoonist Matt Golding has been won for his “Playing Trump” cartoon. Matt Golding Jane Cadzow won Outstanding Feature Writing for “In The Box Seat”, her Good Weekend profile of cardboard king Anthony Pratt, the boss of Visy packaging and one of Australia’s richest men, published in the Herald and The Age. The Age’s veteran crime reporter, John Silvester, also won Outstanding Columnist for his regular Naked City column lifting the lid on Australia’s criminal underworld.



The Herald was nominated for a total of 20 awards, the most of any news organisation in Australia, winning five categories. Related Article Media & marketing Herald scoops young journalist prizes Herald editor Jordan Baker said she was enormously proud of the publication’s winners and finalists. “The recognition of the Herald across so many areas – sport reporting, feature writing, headlines, photography and cartoons – illustrates the depth of talent in our newsroom. “It is also a reflection of the Herald’s commitment to serving our subscribers and telling Sydney’s stories,” Baker said.



The foundation said the 2026 awards attracted a record number of entries. “It’s been another bumper year for excellent Australian journalism, and there’s no greater honour than to receive a Kennedy for your work,” Kennedy Foundation chair Carl Dumbrell said. “The Kennedy Foundation is extremely proud of its support for those endeavours that are essential to an informed and vital democracy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Altona North rocked by second shooting in a week
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaOrganised crime Altona North rocked by second shooting in a week James Costa August 21, 2026 — 10:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been injured in a drive-by shooting outside a cafe in Melbourne’s west. Victoria Police are investigating Friday night’s non-fatal shooting that happened at about 7.15pm on Borrack Square in Altona North. The victim, who is yet to be identified, was taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries. No arrests have been made and police were told the offender or offenders fled the scene in a vehicle. It is the third shooting in Borrack Square this year.



Last week, gangland boss Fadi Haddara was ambushed and shot in the face, stomach and chest outside his Altona North home. Fadi Haddara outside court two years ago. Jason South Haddara, 48, was found lying in a pool of blood by a family member next to a parked car in his driveway on Marigold Avenue, near Millers Road, before 8pm on Sunday. Police said the attack was targeted and are on alert for retaliatory attacks, but are keeping an open mind about the shooting’s connection to Melbourne’s tobacco war. In May, shots were fired into a tobacco store at Borrack square just after 5.30pm.



A 49-year-old man was shot in the arm and taken to a hospital, which police suspected was linked to the Melbourne’s illicit tobacco war. In March, the same square was shot up in a brazen late-night shooting, believed to be linked to the city’s ongoing tobacco war. CCTV footage showed a group of panicked men toppling a table and chairs and running inside to escape the bullets. One man climbed through the cafe’s window, while another two took shelter in corners outside the business. When police arrived, they said they found a 49-year-old man who had been shot twice in the arm. He was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. World.title: Dolphins outclass Eels to stay in top four; Broncos end Raiders’ finals hopes
World.content:
Josh Papali’i’s home-ground swan song has ended in heartache, with Brisbane surging in the second half to overcome an emotional Canberra 34-30.

Papali’i announced that he would retire at the end of the season ahead of the Raiders’ final home game, ending a glittering one-club tenure, in which he played in the 2019 NRL grand final and became the team’s most-capped player (341 games).

Loading

But even after Canberra renamed GIO Stadium “Papa’s House” for Friday’s clash, the home team only led 18-16 at half-time after two Brisbane tries while captain Pat Carrigan was in the sin bin.

The Raiders put themselves in the box seat when hooker Owen Pattie and second-rower Zac Hosking crossed, but two tries in three minutes thrust the visitors back into the contest.

Reece Walsh’s replacement Hayze Perham stormed over in the 73rd minute to edge the Broncos in front, and a try-saving tackle from Josiah Karapani on winger Xavier Savage helped the visitors hang on for the win.

It capped off a dazzling performance for Perham, who provided a lofting try assist to Grant Anderson in the first half and nailed five from six conversion attempts.

An investigation that revealed the NRL’s top referee had a gambling problem, photographs capturing the Bondi Beach terror attack, and a profile of Australia’s cardboard king are part of the Herald’s award-winning coverage celebrated at the Kennedy Foundation’s Excellence in Journalism awards. Edwina Pickles has been recognised for her photographic coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack. Photographer Edwina Pickles won the Outstanding News Photography category for her coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack in December.



Deputy state topic editor Michael Ruffles won the Outstanding Three Headlines category. Cartoonist Matt Golding picked up the Outstanding Cartoon award for “Playing Trump”, which depicted Russian President Vladimir Putin passing the dice to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the pair play a board game called “Trump” with North Korea’s Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Cartoonist Matt Golding has been won for his “Playing Trump” cartoon. Matt Golding Jane Cadzow won Outstanding Feature Writing for “In The Box Seat”, her Good Weekend profile of cardboard king Anthony Pratt, the boss of Visy packaging and one of Australia’s richest men, published in the Herald and The Age. World.title: MBIE backs council ruling that Christchurch Airbnb owners need to get consent or stop
World.content:
The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) has ruled that Christchurch unit owners have to ask for permission to offer the property as an Airbnb - or stop.

Christchurch City Council sought a determination from the ministry because it felt the owners, named in the determination as T Denman and K Suter, had changed the use of the unit from its consented use as a household unit, by making it available for short-term accommodation.

The unit, on Gloucester St, was issued a code compliance certificate in May 2025 as a multi-unit dwelling.

It is on the ground floor with a separate unit above.

The council told MBIE that it did not have evidence the unit had ever been used for its consented use and had been advertised online as visitor accommodation. The unit could be booked for one group at a time and one night or more.

The council contacted the owners in March telling them that the unit had changed from a residential classification to accommodation.

They had breached two requirements of the Building Act, in that they should have given notice of change of use, and that they could not change the use of the building unless the council gave them written notice that the new use would comply with the relevant provisions of the building code.

It issued a notice to fix, which said the owners should notify the council of the change, supply required documentation, and receive written notice that the new use would comply with the rules as required.

Alternatively, they would have to stop using the building for accommodation and return it to its residential use.

The owners said they had sought advice from the council before they started letting the unit and were told it would not be considered a change of use.

They had told the council they wanted to make it a short-term rental so they could use it as a holiday home.

MBIE principal adviser determinations Rebecca Mackie said there was no dispute the council had not approved a change.

There was also no dispute that the multi-unit residential building was consented as sleeping residential.

The question was whether the use had changed.

Mackie found that it had, because the unit was advertised at a nightly rate.

"In this case, the unit is not occupied as the exclusive home or residence of a household... The unit is made available to members of the public as short-term accommodation through an online accommodation platform, with different occupants able to stay on a nightly or weekly basis. That pattern of occupation is transient, rotational and commercial in character. Although each booking may involve only one person or one group staying at a time, there is no continuity of occupation by any particular household.

"The purpose of the use is to rent the unit out as temporary accommodation. That use is materially different from the purpose of the Housing category.... nor do I consider the low level of services provided is determinative of the use of the unit."

Mackie said the unit's use group had changed and there were additional or more onerous building code requirements with the new rules.

"The owners did not provide written notice to the authority under section 114, and the use was changed without written notice from the authority under section 115 that the building in its new use complies to the extent required, in contravention of these sections of the Act. Therefore, there was a basis to issue the notice to fix under section 164."

She upheld the council's notice to fix.

Consultant Mike Blackburn said the determination was relevant to apartments in other developments that were used predominantly as short-term accommodation.

"Where Council determines that a change of use has occurred, the Building Act process can also bring additional Building Code requirements into consideration. In this case MBIE specifically identified requirements relating to access and facilities for people with disabilities as an example of requirements applying to the new use. For developers, designers, property owners and operators involved in this part of the market, Determination 2026/026 is therefore one worth being aware of."

World.title: Hamilton man Jason Monkley charged childcare firm $2900 to fix van - then torched it
World.content:
A man who was trusted to repair a childcare van instead drove it to Hamilton Gardens and set it alight, only to be caught by his own CCTV footage.

Jason Paul Monkley had spent months fixing the Ōtorohanga-based Kiwi Kids Club van.

The owner had shelled out $2900 for materials, but after telling her the work was done and he would take it for a warrant, Monkley instead drove the van to Hamilton Gardens in the dead of night and torched it.

His actions led to a charge of arson, and this week Monkley appeared in Hamilton District Court for sentencing before Judge Stephen Clark.

Court documents state Monkley twice denied any involvement in the blaze. However, his movements were tracked to the minute by the city council, BP and his own CCTV system.

The court heard the victim had arranged for Monkley to fix her company van in mid to late 2024. Over the following months, she paid $2900 for the work to be completed.

By 13 May, 2025, the van was ready to be picked up. Monkley contacted the victim and said he needed to take it for a warrant of fitness.

However, at 3.02am on 15 May, Monkley was spotted on his CCTV system leaving his house with a red petrol container in his Ford.

He was caught on CCTV at BP Whitiora 20 minutes later, before he returned home.

At 4.46am, he was seen putting a bike and a clear plastic container into the back of the van before driving off.

He drove through Gate 1 at Hamilton Gardens at 5.32am and parked the van near the main car park. He set it on fire soon after and then rode his bike home.

Police received a call about the fire at 5.51am from a member of the public.

When spoken to, Monkley denied any involvement and said the van was stolen from outside his house.

He was questioned a second time and told officers he had left it outside an associate's property, from where it was stolen.

Monkley, a sickness beneficiary, had earlier accepted a sentence indication, and his counsel Glen Prentice said nothing in a pre-sentence report suggested he was unsuitable for home detention. He had been on bail with no issues, and he could immediately pay the reparation of $3400, which included a $500 insurance excess.

Judge Clark read excerpts from the victim impact statement in which she said she had trusted Monkley.

She ran the childcare programme in Te Kūiti and Ōtorohanga "with little to no support from the community" and was "flabbergasted" by his actions.

While Monkley's motive was not discussed in court, the victim said he could have told her he was "having issues".

"She says she was somewhat stunned and disappointed, and you could have worked it out as she described you as a family friend."

Judge Clark said he could not see anything in his pre-sentence report that would warrant further credit, except perhaps the fact Monkley had offered to pay the reparation in full.

For that, and his plea, the judge sentenced Monkley to nine months' home detention from a starting point of 19 months' jail.

The judge ordered the reparation be paid within 14 days.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: East Coast conservationist rescues emu chicks after feral cat attack
World.content:
An East Coast conservationist has become a surrogate dad to a couple of emu chicks, rescuing them after a feral cat attacked their nest.

Ruatoria man Graeme Atkins took the chicks in after inadvertently scaring away their real father.

"I was down the beach collecting firewood for a birthday celebration and scared the dad off the nest," he told Checkpoint.

"It was a bit of a bummer that that happened," he said, explaining that male emus look after the eggs and raise the chicks.

After a restless night spent worrying about the birds, he returned to the nest and saw a feral cat had attacked.

"Out of the five chicks I saw the day before only two were left," he said.

So he took action, taking them in despite "a little bit of trepidation about what we were getting into".

The chicks have made themselves at home on Atkins' property. Supplied

Raising them was similar to raising puppies, he said, as the chicks squeaked beside him.

"We've got so much advice from people who know emus.

"They're pretty endearing as a pet, they grow on you," he said.

The chicks are three weeks old now, and spend their days following Atkins around. He has created a warm home for them in a fenced-in enclosure outside his house.

"Because it's been so cold I put them inside a box that's got wool matting, and then some dry grass."

They have quickly made themselves at home - and developed a taste for some of the rare plants on Atkins' property.

"In six months they could be up to five feet tall," he said.

World.title: ACT to campaign on Paul Henry's 'Starship for cancer' proposal
World.content:
The ACT Party wants to build New Zealand's first dedicated national cancer centre, turning a musing from new candidate Paul Henry into a campaign promise.

ACT would establish a philanthropic foundation to attract some of the funding, and get rid of a cap on donation tax credits - the same cap that put one National MP at odds with his party.

When he announced his candidacy in July, Henry said he wanted a world-class cancer hospital in New Zealand, but admitted it would cost "multiple billions" of dollars.

"I think you could easily get a group of wealthy New Zealanders to stump up with about 10 billion, easily. The rest of it we would borrow, but that would be an investment in New Zealand's future," he said at the time.

Now, the party has confirmed it is pressing ahead with the idea, unveiling a plan to build a "Starship for Cancer" with campuses in Auckland and Christchurch.

"Starship showed what New Zealand can achieve when we concentrate talent, technology, generosity and national ambition around a single mission. ACT wants to do the same for cancer," Henry said.

Henry said Starship Children's Hospital in Auckland showed what the country could achieve when it concentrated on a single mission. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

The former broadcaster confessed he had announced the policy "on the fly" last month, and had expected to be pulled aside and discouraged.

"Instead I was told, 'we think you might be onto something'," he told an audience in Christchurch.

ACT expected around $2 billion of capital investment would be required.

"When I mentioned this out of the blue standing next to David Seymour at the press conference, I suggested we might be looking at a figure close to $10 billion, so ACT's involvement has already saved the country $8 billion," Henry said.

ACT would legislate to establish a not-for-profit, independent National Cancer Centre Foundation with charitable status.

To attract donations, ACT would remove the cap on donation tax credits.

The cap was criticised by National MP Greg Fleming on Thursday, who said work was underway to "fix" it, but revenue minister Simon Watts has insisted there are no plans to change it.

A policy document explained the centres would be funded through a combination of public-private partnership financing, charitable donations, existing Crown health investment, and other private capital "where appropriate".

The Department of Cancer Sciences at the University of Auckland and the Christchurch Cancer Foundation would work on business cases for the campuses.

Henry admitted he announced the policy "on the fly". RNZ

Health New Zealand would be a "major customer" of the centre, with ACT expecting it would relocate its existing cancer services in Auckland and Christchurch to the new campuses.

The Crown's ongoing financial liability would come through Health New Zealand purchasing the clinical services and using the facilities.

"This expenditure, to a significant extent, would otherwise need to occur elsewhere in the health system. In the future, medical

tourism from overseas could help subsidise the Centre's operations," the document said.

Henry said the campaign policy was "aspirational" but insisted it was realistic and practical.

"Comprehensive cancer centres are the gold standard internationally because they bring researchers, clinicians, universities, private providers and philanthropists together with world-class treatment, technology and clinical trials," he said.

World.title: Lawyer convicted of assault on his 12-year-old son which left him hospitalised
World.content:
A lawyer has been convicted and granted name suppression following a serious assault on his son that required him being hospitalised.

The lawyer, aged in his 50s, appeared in the Timaru District Court on Friday before Judge Campbell Savage where he was sentenced to supervision after pleading guilty to a charge of assault on a child.

The judge said the case, which began in 2022, had moved at "glacial pace".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Court documents obtained by RNZ detail the offending which occurred in April 2022.

The summary of facts said the lawyer and his son were boxing on a concrete area at the rear of their address.

The lawyer was a "fully grown man and the victim is a small built, 38kg 12-year-old child," the summary said.

Both were wearing boxing gloves.

The lawyer struck the victim's head causing him to bleed.

"The victim said 'please stop. I am serious'.

"The defendant then struck the victim in the face followed by the stomach. This caused the victim to cry. He went to the ground.

"The defendant continued to punch the victim on the ground. Eventually the victim said he could not breath and the defendant stopped. The victim then jumped the fence to get away."

The victim was taken to hospital and was initially diagnosed with a suspected fractured cheekbone and perforated liver, however after scans this was not the case.

He sustained extensive bruising to his head and ears and a cut above his eye.

He was admitted to hospital for three nights to allow observation and investigation of his possible injuries.

The lawyer declined to comment to police.

At sentencing the man's lawyer, Michael Sandom told the court the lawyer appeared before the court as a defendant and as a practicing lawyer.

The lawyer was convicted at Timaru District Court. (File photo) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Sandom said he was appearing among many of his colleagues and peers, which brought a level of "embarrassment and shame".

"[He] is not a perfect person, but none of us are.

"He knows the mistake that he made, he is remorseful for what occurred and in my submission shame for what occurred is an important theme for this sentencing."

Sandom said the offending would stay with the lawyer "for the rest of his life".

The offending was "distressing and repugnant" to the lawyer.

"He's ashamed for what occurred. He can barely face it, can barely talk about it, can barely engage with it at all."

Sandom said the lawyer was a "kind and generous person" as well as an "advocate" in the criminal jurisdiction.

He accepted it was "serious" offending.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae said the Crown opposed the lawyer's application for a discharge without conviction and said his affidavit for name suppression did not meet the threshold.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae. (File photo) Stuff / Pool / Alden Williams

Judge Savage said the matter had passed through the court system "at glacial pace", with the first hearing in April 2022.

The lawyer pleaded guilty during a trial after the victim had given evidence. Judge Savage said the lawyer's claim he did not see his son's statement until trial was "implausible".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Judge Savage said it was "charitable" to say the lawyer's guilty plea came at the 11th hour.

"It came as the clock was striking 12."

He said he had no doubt the lawyer loved his son "with all your heart".

In terms of aggravating factors, the judge pointed to the victim's age and the breach of trust.

Judge Savage declined to discharge the lawyer without a conviction, but did grant final name suppression.

He said he did not see the lawyer as a risk of re-offending.

The lawyer has been practicing for more than a decade. The New Zealand Law Society register does not say whether he holds a practicing certificate.

RNZ asked the New Zealand Law Society how the lawyer was able to continue practicing while the matter was before the court.

A spokesperson said the Law Society took any concerns regarding criminal offending by lawyers "seriously".

"Personal conduct by a lawyer may be considered under the complaints and disciplinary framework in the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006 (the Act) in certain circumstances.

"However, a lawyer who holds a current practising certificate and admits to, or is found guilty of, criminal offending is not automatically suspended from practice."

The spokesperson said concerns or complaints must first be considered by independent Standards Committees who may refer matters to the New Zealand Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal, if the conduct was "sufficiently serious".

"In addition, section 40 of the Act provides that a lawyer who has applied to renew their practising certificate may continue to practise while the application is being considered. This may include cases where proceedings are ongoing."

Asked if a lawyer could be suspended pending a complaint, the spokesperson said only the tribunal could make an order that a lawyer be suspended from practice, including for an interim period while any disciplinary process is underway, or strike a lawyer off the roll of barristers and solicitors following referral from a Standards Committee.

The Disciplinary Tribunal is administered by the Ministry of Justice.

Asked why the register did not have the expiry date for the lawyer's practising certificate, the spokesperson said the Society was unable to comment on individual cases for privacy reasons.

"Speaking generally, practising certificates have an expiry date of 30 June each year."

Ministry of Justice acting group manager of National Service Delivery Louisa Carroll said the Ministry could not comment on the circumstances of any individual lawyer or active court proceedings.

Asked about the lawyer receiving legal aid clients, Carroll said legal aid providers must meet and maintain approval requirements and comply with the Legal Services Act, their legal aid provider contract, and professional obligations.

"Legal aid providers are also required to notify the Ministry within five working days if they are charged with, or convicted of, an offence punishable by imprisonment."

"Where the Ministry becomes aware of concerns about a provider, it may consider those concerns through its complaints, audit, quality assurance and provider approval processes."

Carroll said depending on the circumstances, the Ministry may take a range of actions, including imposing restrictions on a provider, modifying or cancelling their approval to undertake legal aid work, or referring matters to the New Zealand Law Society.

"Approved providers remain eligible to receive legal aid assignments unless their approval is changed, restricted, suspended, or cancelled.

World.title: Healthline calls in reinforcements amid biggest flu outbreak in 10 years
World.content:
Healthline calls in reinforcements for flu surge Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Healthline has called in reinforcements to cope with a deluge of calls amid the biggest flu outbreak in years.

Flu-related hospitalisations are at a 10-year high in Auckland, with national infection rates at a four-year high and rising.

Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley earlier said the entire health system was under pressure, with the spike being driven by influenza A along with cases of RSV, cold viruses and some Covid-19 cases.

The chief operating officer of Wakarongorau Aotearoa, which operates Healthline, Brian O'connell, told Checkpoint the service was handling about 20 percent more calls in the past seven days compared to July.

He said a normal day would see about 1000 calls but this was now up to 1200 to 1300 a day.

Healthline had increased resourcing by about 10 percent, he said. This meant at any time there were about 25 nurses and paramedics on and the current wait time was 10 minutes.

"When people are calling Healthline they're connected with one of our nurses or paramedics and can talk through concerns and then our team will work with them about how urgently they need to seek health advice or give advice to keep themselves well at home."

Out of every five people Healthline spoke to, O'connell said only one would be diverted through to hospital or calling 111.

He said Healthline could be especially helpful at the moment for any parent who was worried about a sick child.

"Speaking to our clincial team can really help give you that reassurance and make sure you're not going to the wrong place."

About 30 percent of the calls Healthline received were for children under the age of 5.

As a result, O'connell said Plunket had been helping out by putting on more nurses who could take calls relating to young children.

Plunket told Checkpoint in a statement, it was taking an extra 200 calls a day as it helped to support Healthline with addressing demand.

It said some whānau might experience longer wait times than usual.

How can the flu outbreak be addressed?

Should people be masking up as flu outbreaks surge? Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

University of Otago professor of Public Health Dr Michael Baker told Checkpoint, more needed to be done sooner in the future, including stronger advice about masks.

"The problem is when we're at this stage of the epidemic curve we've left it too late because we're already overwhelming the health system. It's hard to change the trajectory."

Professor of Public Health Dr Michael Baker. (File photo) Supplied / Department of Public Health

He said a graded response to dampen down transmission would be a good idea along with continuing with vaccination.

"But now we're stuck in this situation and I hope we can do better in future.

Winter respiratory infections usually went from May to October, Baker said, with the intensity varying greatly year-to-year.

Baker said we needed to get better at rapidly ramping up control measures including mask use in enclosed environments and additional precautions in high risk settings like public transport and waiting rooms.

Employers could also get more active at discouraging workers from coming to work sick, he said, and encourage working from home.

There were also additional RAT tests available now that could test for influenza, RSV and Covid-19, Baker said, which were tools available to be used in strategic ways.

"Some countries do have systems for communicating the level of respiratory risk in the community. We don't have a graded system in place to know when to issue those warnings - a system like this needs a bit of design work, working with community groups, Māori and those that are particularly vulnerable to get a sense of the kinds of warnings they would appreciate.

"We've published work in the past about having a graded system on this for seasonal infections...it's quite a well established approach but we do need that willingness from our political and health leaders."

World.title: Report on Mt Maunganui landslide risk unread: Tauranga City Council
World.content:
Tauranga councillors had report outlining landslide risk Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Tauranga councillors had a detailed report showing there was a high risk people could die if their local campground got hit by a landslide but no one read the report.

The council said that despite the report being in an August 2025 council agenda, it was not read and the meeting never happened.

Five months after the meeting was cancelled, six people were killed in a landslide as debris came off Mount Maunganui and covered a large area of the campground.

Retired High Court Justice Paul Davison KC found information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed, forwarded and then left.

But on Wednesday, when his report was released, council chief executive Marty Grenfell told RNZ that no senior staff saw those reports.

"These reports were never escalated to a point where anybody at a senior level within the organisation could provide guidance, direction, and ensure that they were appropriately managed."

Grenfell said the reports stayed at "operational level".

"Our systems were such that from an organisation perspective, we weren't aware that these reports were being commissioned."

However, the council's own website showed that a June 2025 geo hazard report was included in an August agenda.

It says the rock stability monitoring report was sent out along with the meeting agenda, but the meeting was cancelled so none of the councillors actually read it.

The chief executive's name is on the agenda's cover, but in a statement the council said this did not mean he read the information either.

A council spokesperson said the report itself cost more than $12,000. They said the meeting was cancelled because of concerns about the number of councillors able to attend, but they were not sure why it was never rescheduled.

Call for accountability

Local group Lobby for Good spokesperson Erika Harvey said it was even more concerning that the information was circulated but never read.

"How do you think the families feel now? Now, not only did they know, not only could they have prevented it, but actually nobody actually cared to read it.

"You cannot tell me that this is just something that you should say, oh well, we'll learn next time from this. This is worse than a systemic failure. This is a governance failure. This is, in my opinion, this is negligence.

"If no one's reading anything and you can just use that as an excuse not to know what's going on, when you're paid more than the Prime Minister - over $600,000 Marty gets paid, more than the Prime Minister - to run a town, a city. Could you imagine if the Prime Minister said that? Oh sorry, we didn't know. I didn't get the report and six people died."

She said she had lost faith in the system and that someone needed to be held accountable.

"Now there's a document that says it could have been prevented, along with a report, and here's how much it could have been prevented but now nobody read it."

Echoes of CTV collapse

It brought back memories for a man whose wife died in the collapse of the CTV building during the 2011 Christchurch earthquake.

Maan Alkaisi from the CTV Families Group said they also waited for answers, accountability and justice but that the councillors failing to read their own report was proof that local government was not learning from previous failings.

"That really of course resonates with what happened with the CTV, because there were two reports explicitly highlighting a risk of collapse in case of earthquake and yet no action was taken."

He said it was disappointing and concerning that after 15 years nothing appeared to have changed.

"The whole idea from all these investigations, royal commissions, and police and ... WorkSafe and all that - they conduct investigations and they make recommendations and then none of these recommendations [have] actually been followed up or implemented, and we risk more people and more people lose their lives, and we know that this is preventable.

World.title: Third case of H5 bird flu found in Wellington region
World.content:
A third case of H5 bird flu has been detected in a northern giant petrel, in the Wairarapa.

Ministry for Primary Industries says it was found dead on a remote Cape Palliser beach.

It follows cases found in a kāhu, or swamp harrier, and a brown skua.

It was found by a Department of Conservation (DOC) ranger, who notified the MPI hotline.

Samples received by the MPI Animal Health Laboratory on 14 August were tested and initially found low levels of influenza virus in the bird. It took several rounds of testing to confirm bird flu.

MPI chief veterinary officer Mary van Andel said this latest case had not come as a shock.

"Although it's disappointing to find one of these infected birds, it's really not surprising.

"We can definitely expect to have more of these ocean-going seabirds arrive in New Zealand. We know that they come here. We know that birds in the Southern Ocean are infected with clade 2.3.4.4b."

Dr van Andel said chicken and eggs were absolutely safe to eat and there were no food safety concerns.

"This is a single detection in an ocean-going seabird, so no spread in New Zealand wildlife detected, no detections in poultry in New Zealand, and so really not much has changed."

She asked people to report any sightings of sick or dead birds to MPI.

"What we need is for people who see groups of sick or dying birds to report those.

World.title: Brisbane boys go back to back with stunning come-from-behind wins
World.content:
Brisbane has mounted a stunning second-half fightback to deny Josh Papali'i a win in his final game at Canberra Stadium before the Dolphins shook off another slow start to take down the Eels.

The loss ended the Raiders' faint finals hopes after they looked on track for a celebratory victory while leading 30-16 with 18 minutes left in the retiring Papali'i's hometown farewell.

But 18 straight points, capped saw the Broncos to a 34-30 win in scenes reminiscent of their comeback win at the same ground in last year's finals series, albeit in much lower stakes and far more conventional fashion.

At Lang Park, the Dolphins consolidated their place in the league's top four with a 34-16 win over the Eels after they too trailed 10-0 after just 20 minutes.

The Dolphins have made a habit of relying on their sparkling attack to fire them back from slow starts, and it has now carried them to five straight wins and four points clear of Cronulla in fourth spot.

Look back at all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: Australia names team for second Test against Bangladesh
World.content:
Australia have resisted the temptation to play four specialist fast bowlers against Bangladesh in the second Test in Mackay, as captain Pat Cummins confirmed Matt Renshaw would open the batting.

The recalled Renshaw is a straight swap for Jake Weatherald, who was dropped after six underwhelming Test matches.

The pitch at Great Barrier Reef Arena is expected to assist the pacemen, but off spinner Nathan Lyon, after taking 1-102 in the first innings of the nine-wicket loss by Australia in Darwin, will play his 143rd Test.

Australia vs Bangladesh second Test preview Winter cricket continues in the Top End, with Australia looking for a big response in the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay.

Outstanding paceman Scott Boland did not play in Darwin and will now have to wait until the tour of South Africa in October for his next Test, after starring in last summer's Ashes.

Pitch curator Peter Kazakoff said the Mackay wicket would suit fast bowlers on both sides.

"That is what we are aiming for, a lot of pace," he said.

"We want the ball to come through really nicely. We have got the same sort of clay as the Gabba, so we are expecting similar sort of characteristics to that."

Australia confirmed their side, with Lyon in it, an hour after captain Cummins held a press conference where he said he was considering an all-out pace attack.

Kazakoff said there would be a role for Lyon and the Bangladesh spinners.

"I think the spinners will come into the game, going off previous first-class games here," he said.

"Spinners have had a big say later in the match. Obviously those first-class games were a bit later in the year when it was a bit warmer.

"It is a lot cooler this time of year. The moisture will come out of the wicket less and slower."

There has been a lot of talk about "soul-searching" in the Australian camp after the Darwin loss, but Cummins said he was confident of a response.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

"In home Test matches we pride ourselves on winning as many as we can," he said.

"It's funny. I think if we played really well and we lost you'd feel like we needed to do some soul-searching.

"I certainly felt like we didn't play anywhere near our best and they played really well. When we play well, fortunately we have got a decent body of work to look back on."

Weatherald's axing was simple to explain for Cummins, who said he was "awesome around the group" but did not deliver.

"Over the course of six Test matches he didn't quite score the runs he or we would have liked," Cummins said.

Renshaw, 30, will play his first Test in three years after averaging 49.9 in Sheffield Shield cricket last summer, including scoring three centuries.

"[Renshaw] has been really impressive and had some great off-season tours of Pakistan and Bangladesh recently with white-ball (formats). He looks in good nick," Cummins said.

"He had a really good Shield season last season.

"Some of the kind of chat about [Renshaw] in the past is that he can look different from day to day.

"When you get to the back half of your career as a batter you want to really know what you look like at your best, and I think he does that.

"I hope he brings his best version every day, is nice and sharp and puts the pressure on the bowlers."

Australia XI for second Test: Matthew Renshaw, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey (wk), Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (c), Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood

AAP

World.title: Swans AFLW captain and coach say club is 'united' amid scandal
World.content:
Sydney Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy has said her players have had "open conversations" in the wake of the scandal that has engulfed her club and led to five men's players being suspended for the rest of the season.

McEvoy, along with AFLW coach Colin O'Riordan, spoke to the media on Friday afternoon, saying the women's program supports the sanctions imposed on Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. The press conference has ended AFLW players would like to have say in whether five suspended men's players return Lucy McEvoy is asked if the AFLW players have discussed whether they want the five suspended players to return to the club. She tells the media that conversation has not happened but, when the time comes, the AFLW players would like to be part of the discussion. 'Moment for all women to stand together', McEvoy Here is more from Lucy McEvoy, speaking about the wider issue at the heart of this week's scandal. "There's no doubt, I think, a lot of women in the community are all feeling the same. "It's obviously an issue within the community that needs to be addressed, and I think this week it has been. "I applaud the club in the way they have handled it, and respected us as a women's program. "I think it's an important moment for all women to stand together and understand that all women deserve respect." Show more

Those five players will miss the remainder of the AFL season following club-imposed suspensions for breaking team standards in Melbourne earlier this week.

Victoria Police are investigating a sexual assault allegation, where it is alleged one player touched a woman without her consent. No charges have been laid, and no-one has been formally interviewed.

Speaking on Friday, McEvoy said the AFLW program supported the club-imposed suspensions to the five men's players, and said their actions did not reflect the Swans as a club.

"On behalf of the playing group, we also support the club in the sanctions that were handed down," McEvoy said.

"To the players, we are incredibly disappointed, as a lot of people were.

"We know that the actions of those five players are not a reflection of the broader club."

McEvoy said it had been a big week for the women's program, who will face Essendon at the Sydney Cricket Ground this weekend.

The Swans were hoping to celebrate this week's double-header with the men's round 24 clash with North Melbourne following the AFLW match on Sunday afternoon.

In the wake of this week's scandal, McEvoy said members of the women's program were processing their emotions and the situation.

"We've had some really open conversations as a group this week, and with the club more broadly," she said.

"We've felt the support both internally and externally as well.
