"The girls are working through their emotions as they see fit for themselves."

When asked how this week has affected the reputation of the Sydney Swans, McEvoy said the club, both men's and women's teams, must work to regain the public's trust.

"There's no doubt the club has taken a reputational hit," she said.

"We will do whatever we can as a club, both programs, to make sure we build back the trust and respect of our members and fans, and the community more broadly."

O'Riordan, who played 34 AFL matches for the Swans between 2015 and 2022 before becoming the club's AFLW coach this season, said he was disappointed that he had to address this scandal.

"The actions of a small number of people have impacted a lot of people, especially the women in our football club and wider community," he said.

"As a man who was brought up with strong morals and a strong sense of what is right and wrong, [it's] disappointing to be standing here today and be talking about something like this.

"Growing up, I was always taught you treat everyone with respect, and that respect is a fundamental pillar of how you live your life.

"That is especially important in how you treat women."

O'Riordan said the club had remained "incredibly united" in the wake of the scandal.

"This is a united club. It always has been and always will be," he said.

World.title: Panthers NRL finals charge dealt blow by Cogger's three-match ban
World.content:
Penrith is in for a NRL finals selection dilemma after key addition Jack Cogger received a three-match ban for his high shot on Tyran Wishart.

Just when the streaky Panthers looked to have found their best option at five-eighth, Cogger received a grade-two charge that rules him out until after the first week of finals.

Unless Cogger can plead his case at the judiciary and win, the Panthers will be forced to recall out-of-favour Blaize Talagi or Perth-bound Jack Cole.

Storm's finals dream over as Penrith holds on despite triple sin-binning The Penrith Panthers hold on to beat the Melbourne Storm 22-14 and end their faint mathematical hopes of making the NRL finals.

Cogger was sent to the sin bin after rushing out of the line to hit Wishart late in the Panthers' 22-14 win on Thursday night.

He has already been suspended once this season for a similar shot, missing two weeks on that occasion for rushing out and hitting South Sydney's Ashton Ward.

If he unsuccessfully challenges his charge at the judiciary, Cogger will miss an additional game, potentially ruling him out for the remainder of the season.

Cogger also received a $3,000 fine for a shot on Storm forward Angus Hinchey earlier in the clash.

But the 29-year-old's suspension is a far bigger blow for a Penrith side fighting to lock up a top-two finish.

Cogger has been a valuable addition to the Panthers' starting side in recent weeks, proving a more assured defensive presence than Talagi.

His ball-playing has also helped take pressure off halfback Nathan Cleary, as it did during Penrith's comeback victory in the 2023 grand final.

But Cogger's illegal tackle has now opened the door for either Talagi or Cole, one of whom is set to start in the halves for next week's clash with Canterbury.

AAP

World.title: Swans captain 'deeply shocked' by scandal, denies player rift
World.content:
Sydney Swans coach Dean Cox and captain Callum Mills have denied there is a rift in their playing group as they addressed the ongoing scandal engulfing the club.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Mills said he was "deeply shocked and disappointed" and said he had not witnessed anything like this behaviour before.

"We really are disappointed at the action of these five players," he said.

Dean Cox and Callum Mills addressed the media. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"As a playing group, we fully support the club's decisions on the sanctions handed down."

Mills said the five players would have to address the playing group, but there was no rift among the players.

Cox confirmed he was not in the room at the centre of the scandal, but would not say whether other staff members or players were present, as the club denied comments suggesting more men from the Swans were present in the room.

Both men refused to answer specific questions about what happened in the hotel room, saying they were the subject of a police investigation.

The Swans players and staff observed the press conference from behind the camera. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cox was also pressed on the club's decision to have the five suspended players driven back to Sydney from Melbourne, rather than flown.

"Decisions were made [as to] how we best support our players within the circumstances that happened," he said.

Cox admitted the club's previously acclaimed culture had "taken a hit".

"Our culture isn't perfect," he said.

"We're going to work as hard as we possibly can to get the trust back from the community, to get the culture where we desire to be, where we once had been."

Live Moment Catch up up the key moments from Dean Cox and Callum Mills's press conference from Swans HQ. The press conference is over Dean Cox and Callum Mills have finished answering questions at Swans HQ. Cox's message to Sydney's fans ahead of the weekend Cox is asked what his message is to the club's fans considering coming to this weekend's games. "I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs. "We want to show that on Sunday." Is there concern for the mental health of the players? Mills is asked whether he is concerned for the mental health of the players suspended by the club. "There's concern in every part. That's the women in the community, our players involved, the women involved. "The wellbeing of everyone involved is [of] the utmost importance." Show more

Both Cox and Mills apologised to the club's AFLW team, with Mills saying he had addressed the group personally.

"I acknowledged their pain, and I deeply apologised for the actions of a few within our group," he said.

Cox added that he hoped the supporters would still come out in force for the double-header at the SCG this weekend.

"I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs," he said.

"We want to show that on Sunday."

Sydney's men's team rounds out its home and away season with a clash against North Melbourne on Sunday afternoon at the SCG, a match preceded by an AFLW match between Sydney's women's team and Essendon's women's team at the same venue.

World.title: 'Horrific consequences': Aussie star almost hit by car in Tour of Britain
World.content:
Australian cyclist Maeve Plouffe has revealed she nearly got hit by a car while riding in this week's Tour of Britain — and has warned of potentially more "horrific consequences" for a sport already reeling from tragedy.

Plouffe, the 27-year-old former Sydney track star who grabbed Commonwealth team pursuit gold and individual silver in 2022, prompted organisers of the week-long road race to review safety procedures after she outlined her "scary" experience.

Plouffe had to withdraw from the race, having suffered a puncture during the opening stage in Cumbria on Wednesday, and her revelation on Instagram about an alarming episode with a car as she attempted to chase back to the peloton.

Plouffe posted the statement of her close call on her personal Instagram account. (Instagram/@maeveplouffe)

Her comments came only days after British rider Finlay Tarling died last week during stage eight of the Volta a Portugal after he was hit by a non-race light goods vehicle that had entered the course.

Explaining her withdrawal, Plouffe added: "While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down, there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout.

"Later on, the moto escort was wonderful, and I felt much safer.

"But considering the recent devastating events in our cycling community, it's scary to see situations like this, when we know that this can have horrific consequences, especially so soon after suffering such a tragedy."

She was referring to the death of the 19-year-old Tarling, who was killed last week in a high-speed collision with a van, which had strayed onto the road during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

British rider Finlay Tarling (right) was killed by a non-race light goods vehicle during the Volta a Portugal last week. (Getty Images: Huw Fairclough)

Before the Tour of Britain Women had begun, an emotional tribute was paid to Tarling, with his picture projected onto a large screen while all 114 riders and roadside fans joined in a minute's applause to honour him.

Tarling was the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling, who will ride the Vuelta a España Grand Tour, which begins on Saturday, in honour of his sibling.

Organisers have swiftly taken note of Plouffe with Jonathan Day, events director of British Cycling Ventures — the commercial arm of British Cycling that organises the Tour — saying in a statement: "We're taking those comments extremely seriously."

"Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.

"We're reviewing what happened with Maeve and her team, O'Shea Red Chilli Bikes, with the seriousness and empathy these comments demand.

"We recognise this comes at an especially difficult time for the cycling community, so we want to reassure all riders, teams and fans of the sport at this time of how seriously we are treating these comments."

The race continued on Thursday with Dutch superstar Lorena Wiebes claiming her second successive stage victory between Clitheroe and Blackpool but only after that second stage had been neutralised because of a car accident.

Australian rider Georgia Baker, fresh from her golden Commonwealth Games on the track in Glasgow, was also caught up in a crash on the route.

Wiebes is 14 seconds ahead of Italy's Chiara Consonni (Canyon-SRAM zondacrypto) in the general classification as the race moves into Wales on Friday.

AAP

World.title: Alcaraz confirms US Open return amid record prize money reveal
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz is set to return to action at the US Open, ending four months of injury torment, and will be back competing for a record grand slam winner's prize of $US5.5 million ($7.7 million) in New York.

The news of the seven-time grand slam winner's comeback at Flushing Meadows will be music to the ears of former Australian Open boss Craig Tiley, who has been able to begin his reign in charge of the US Open by announcing unprecedented riches to the players.

Seven-time grand slam champion Alcaraz has not played since April due to a concerning wrist injury.

He announced his return on Thursday in unusual fashion, with the help of football journalist Fabrizio Romano.

Romano, who is usually breaking news of big football transfers, used his catchphrase, "Here we go," to announce Alcaraz's return on Instagram, while the reigning champ repeated the message on X.

Alcaraz, who started the year by winning the Australian Open, has not played since withdrawing from the Barcelona Open in April. He has missed both the ‌French Open and ⁠Wimbledon while his great rival, Jannik Sinner, has largely dominated.

Now he is fit to return to the scene of his first grand slam triumph in 2022, when he became the youngest man to reach world number one in the rankings.

Alcaraz's return is fantastic news for Tiley, the former Tennis Australia CEO who has taken up the equivalent job at the US Tennis Association (USTA) and has been able to announce an overall prize fund of $US108 million — the first time the $US100m barrier has been broken at a slam.

Alcaraz's 2026 season has been cruelled by a wrist injury. (Getty Images: Quality Sport Images/Alvaro Medranda)

It is the biggest prize pot in the sport's history and represents a 20 per cent rise for the second consecutive year.

"This is a significant first step in a multi-year investment in athletes as the US Open continues to be the best economic opportunity for players and the most valuable platform in tennis for players, fans and partners," Tiley said.

"We are proud to deliver record-setting prize money and expanded player benefits as well as providing a new platform to work together with players."

That platform is the formation of a Grand Slam Player Council, which is intended to give players a voice on a range of issues such as prize money.

Organisers hope all this will ward off the kind of player protests that occurred at the French Open and Wimbledon.

The champions' winning cheque will be $US5.5 million, up from the $5 million that Sabalenka and Alcaraz won last year.

Players will earn $US140,000 just for making it into the main draw, while a quarterfinalist earns $US780,000, a semifinalist $US1.45 million and runners-up $US2.8 million.

Meanwhile, there was good news for the Australian challenge following the withdrawal of Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina from the main draw through injury.

It meant Alexei Popyrin was able to be advanced to the main draw and the reciprocal wildcard he had been given by the USTA could instead go to his Australian teammate Dane Sweeny, who will make his Flushing Meadows debut at 25.

That takes the current Australian contingent set to start the action on August 30 to a total of 14 — eight men and six women — with more attempting to make it through next week's qualifying.

AAP

World.title: Test history looms, Renshaw returns as Australia and Bangladesh go again
World.content:
Australia was handed an historic, humbling nine-wicket defeat by Bangladesh in Darwin earlier this week.

It was the first time the Tigers had claimed a Test-match victory in Australia, and will have prompted some serious soul searching for the hosts, who were comprehensively second-best against the world's ninth ranked team.

Tomorrow morning, more history will be made, with Mackay's Harrup Park becoming the 12th Australian venue to host a Test when the teams begin the second and final match of the series.

You can listen to live coverage of the Test on the ABC Listen App, or follow the ABC Sport live blog

What needs to change for Mackay?: ABC Cricket Podcast

Australia has made one change to its squad for the encounter, with Matt Renshaw coming in for Jake Weatherald, while the return of an exciting young quick sees Bangladesh faced with a selection dilemma.

Here's everything you need to know.

When does the second Test begin?

The second Test between Australia and Bangladesh gets underway on Saturday August 22, with the first session of play beginning at 10am AEST in Mackay, QLD.

That is 10am in Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania, 9:30am in South Australia and the Northern Territory (ACST), and 8am in Western Australia (AWST).

These are the session times for the five scheduled days of cricket:

First: 10:00am – 12:00pm AEST (9:30am — 11:30am ACST, 8:00am — 10:00am AWST)

10:00am – 12:00pm AEST (9:30am — 11:30am ACST, 8:00am — 10:00am AWST) Second: 12:40pm – 2:40pm AEST (12:10pm — 2:10pm ACST, 10:40am — 12:40pm AWST)

12:40pm – 2:40pm AEST (12:10pm — 2:10pm ACST, 10:40am — 12:40pm AWST) Third: 3:00pm – 5:00pm AEST (2:30pm — 4:30pm ACST, 1:00pm — 3:00pm AWST)

And an extra half hour of play will almost certainly be tacked on to the end of each day in an attempt to bowl the full compliment of overs.

Background on Australia's newest Test venue

The Great Barrier Reef Arena will become the 12th venue to host a men's Test in Australia. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Mackay's Harrup Park, also known as the Great Barrier Reef Arena, is set to become Australia's 12th Test venue, the first addition to the list since Canberra's Manuka Oval hosted its debut match in 2019.

The venue has hosted just two Sheffield Shield matches and a pair of Australia A fixtures in the past decade, so it is a relatively unknown quantity when it comes to professional red ball cricket.

But it has seen international action in the past, with both Australia's women's and men's teams playing white-ball games there, and the ground held a youth Test between Australia and India last year.

The most recent Shield match at the venue came in October 2023, when, off the back off a mammoth first dig of 9-501d, Queensland completed an innings victory over Victoria.

Renshaw, in-line to play his first Test in three years tomorrow, was the player-of-the-match in that game, scoring 135 to become the only player to hit two First Class centuries at the venue.

Who is playing?

Renshaw returns to the Australian team after a three-year absence. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Australia has made one change to its squad since the first Test, with opening batter Renshaw coming into the playing group at the expense of Weatherald.

Weatherald returned scores of 23 and 0 in front of his home crowd in Darwin, following on from a disappointing debut series against England last summer.

Renshaw comes into the squad as what appears to be a straight swap, with the Queenslander having scored three Shield centuries at the top of the order last season, averaging 49.90.

However, the last of Renshaw's 14 Tests came in the middle order in Delhi three and a half years ago.

Josh Inglis, the only other batter in the squad not to have played in Darwin, is also in the mix for a return to the team, with Marnus Labuschagne continuing to skate on thin ice at No. 3 after scores of 1 and 31 last week.

Cam Green will be looking to push on after his drought-breaking Darwin ton, while Steve Smith will continue his quest for a first-ever Test century against the Tigers.

Scott Boland seems more likely than not to return to the side, with one of the big four of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and Nathan Lyon to be rotated.

Cummins missed much of last summer through injury and didn't bowl at all in Bangladesh's second innings in Darwin.

Green scored his first Test century in over two years in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Given Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto labelled his side's victory in the first Test "the biggest win" in the country's cricketing history, it would feel extremely harsh on any of that Bangladeshi XI missing out on selection for tomorrow's match.

But the return to fitness of pace bowler Shoriful Islam has undoubtedly provided the Bangladeshi selectors with food for thought.

Prior to this series, the towering left-arm quick was an unquestioned member of the tourists' best XI, and could come into the side for tweaker Taijul Islam, with all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz proving in Darwin he's more than capable of acting as his side's frontline spinner.

But there will be no return for lightning-fast young seamer Nahid Rana, who has already returned to Bangladesh to continue his recovery from a side strain.

And it appears that Bangladesh could be without Darwin centurion Tanzid Hasan, who didn't bat in training on Thursday due to a neck issue — Soumya Sarkar, who last played Test cricket in 2021 and whose selection for the tour was described as a "a bit of desperation" by chief selector Habibul Bashar, would be Tanzid's likely replacement.

How to watch and follow the Test

ABC Sport will broadcast live radio coverage of the Test via the ABC Cricket button on ABC Listen, plus on ABC Sport Digital Radio around our AFL and NRL coverage.

The commentary team includes former Australia cricketers Jason Gillespie, Phil Jacques and Xavier Doherty, as well as Corbin Middlemas, Jim Maxwell and Ben Cameron.

ABC Sport will also live blog every ball of the Test.

The match will be broadcast on Channel 7 and Foxtel, and streamed on 7Plus and Kayo Sports.

Tech.title: Tesla sunsets its Solar Roof tiles
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tesla has discontinued Solar Roof, its solar panels designed to look like regular roofing tiles, Electrek reports. Sources “close to the program” told the publication that Tesla has informed its third-party installer network that Solar Roof is no longer available to order, and that only conventional solar panels will be supplied going forward.

While Tesla hasn’t officially announced that it’s sunsetting the product, it’s made several website changes that corroborate the reported discontinuation. The dedicated Solar Roof page (tesla.com/solarroof) that launched almost a decade ago now automatically redirects to Tesla’s solar panel page instead, and the “Solar Roof” option is no longer available under the navigation menu for Tesla Energy products. The only products currently listed are Solar Panels, Powerwall, and Megapack.

Tesla first revealed the Solar Roof project back in 2016, but only achieved mass production in March 2020. It was never a successful venture for Tesla — CEO Elon Musk admitted in 2021 that the company made “significant mistakes” with Solar Roof that caused over-expenditure and delays, and a Wood Mackenzie report from 2023 estimated that the solar shingles had only been installed on 3,000 US homes since launch — far fewer than Tesla’s target of 1,000 installations per week.

Electrek reports that Tesla has now concluded that Solar Roof is not financially viable for the company. It is, however, seeing greater success with its regular solar panels, and is currently planning to build a new $10 billion factory near Houston, Texas, to ramp up production.

Tech.title: My cats hate each other, but this automatic feeder is helping
Tech.content:
is a senior tech and policy editor focused on online platforms and free expression. Adi has covered virtual and augmented reality, the history of computing, and more for The Verge since 2011.

Over the course of nearly a decade, my husband and I have dutifully carried out a four-times-daily ritual of feeding a pair of lovely cat siblings who hate each other. This was mostly manageable for years, but in 2024, disaster struck for my small dependents: We had a child. Suddenly, the cats were no longer our first priority. Despite our best efforts, their dry-food snack times began slipping or getting missed altogether. It was time, we decided, to turn to the pet-tech industry and hope automated feeders could deliver the attention we couldn’t.

Four machines and a few hundred dollars later, our hope has proven mostly well founded— though no technology can cure the darkness of the feline soul. And as a bonus, my travails have helped me accept being a cheap, lazy shopper in the age of optimization.

There’s a responsible process for getting home goods in the 2020s. Type “[PRODUCT CATEGORY] wirecutter” in a Google search box. Click the handful of reputable outlets that come up: the Wirecutter, of course, but also places like The Strategist. Sort through the set of features that will best suit your needs at the correct price point. Read about the unexpected pain points. Make a well-informed decision. Ideally, wait for a sale.

The less responsible process is to go to Amazon, type in a few keywords, and click “buy” on something in your budget range that doesn’t have a slew of terrible reviews. We were already dedicating hours to finding precisely the best version of every sometimes multi-hundred-dollar purchase for our baby. My brainpower was devoted to studying the tradeoffs between several subtly different categories of stroller. Guess which path we took.

The one thing we really needed to account for was our cats’ personality disorders. Our big orange man, who is either sweetly timid or remarkably charming around any human he encounters, is a swaggering bully who will gobble food until he vomits and appears to resent the fact that his tortoiseshell sister exists. Over the years, his constant looming has driven her to neurosis — no matter how often we chase him away, she eats like a hunted fugitive sneaking bites of food between glances over her shoulder. You can’t feed them too far apart or they’ll both converge on the closest dish, but they must be separated by at least one door (which crucially can only be closed after the commencement of feeding, or the tortie will see it as a sign of danger and flee), so from the get-go, those elegant two-cat feeders were out.

When my cats are together, only one of them gets to eat. Image: Adi Robertson / The Verge

Beyond that, I had a vague sense that our cats would probably attack any weak point in a feeder, and that anything requiring an app was a nonstarter — so we scanned for the simplest and sturdiest thing we could dig up. We were sold on a then-roughly $90 PetSafe programmable feeder by a review promising it was raccoon-resistant, which seemed like a good indicator of quality despite the fact that our cats live entirely indoors.

Two of these feeders — simple black plastic tubs attached to an aluminum bowl — absolutely solved our basic problem. The cats started getting fed more regularly. And while I was braced for a siege situation as they found ways to get extra food out, turns out they simply aren’t that hungry or that smart.

But the feeders themselves became a point of constant, low-level irritation. They each run on four D batteries, which last a long time but basically require turning the feeders upside down when they do need replacing, an exercise in pure annoyance. The five-button interface is, even by the standards of pre-touchscreen systems, so abstruse that I’m the only one with the frustration tolerance to handle it. There’s a command to initiate immediate release of a food portion, but, as far as I can tell, only by skipping the next scheduled feeding. (To make things worse, they use a food treadmill that requires several turns to work kibble through their system if it ever runs dry.) The minimum portion is just slightly too big. Their clocks drift out of sync, creating gaps that let our orange bully finish his meal and rush over to bogart his sister’s. Perhaps most egregiously, that treadmill rumbles gratingly every time it goes off — loud enough to jolt our daughter out of her bedtime routine if feedings fall during it.

In case it’s not abundantly clear, I’ve developed an almost irrational peevishness toward these functionally perfectly adequate products. And it’s shared enough by my family that we’ve tried to improve our circumstances! Last year, we tried again with a pair of roughly $55 automatic feeders from a company called VOLUAS, one of those interchangeable-sounding all-caps Amazon storefronts, which seemed to solve essentially all our problems. The new feeders plugged into the wall with batteries for backup. Their silicone wheel design was quiet enough to not annoy us yet just loud enough for our cats to hear. The smallest portion was exactly large enough. The interface was, if not intuitive, a little less painfully arcane. It had a button to dispense extra portions instantly. It even looked more elegant: a neat rectangular prism with a translucent top for checking the quantity of food still in it, instead of something that looked a bit like a garbage bin.

I’ve developed an almost irrational peevishness toward these functionally perfectly adequate products.

This would all be fantastic if we hadn’t left them in storage for a while, some food still in them, while traveling. We returned to two messy piles of mouse-chewed silicone and two inoperable feeding wheels. Back to the sturdy but unloved PetSafes we went.

For several months now, my husband has been suggesting we simply order more of the new feeders. I keep insisting that the ones we have still work — all I’ve got to do is, somehow, fix this one part! The VOLUAS website has an email address for support, and I keep meaning to ask about a replacement for those little silicon wheels. But my situation is just tenable enough that I keep putting it off. The old feeders work… fine, and may well last the rest of my cats’ lifetimes. The ones I like better are so close to functional it feels wasteful to buy replacements. I’m so accustomed to cat feeder purgatory I’ve almost forgotten paradise.

I imagine my cats feel similarly resigned, to both my diminished free time for cuddling and to each other. After two years, the charming orange man has developed a rapport with our toddler, who’s slowly learning to pet his fur the right direction. Our tortie is still terrified of her, but has put faith in impregnable fortresses like Exact Center of Under the Bed and Chair Turned Toward the Wall, where she’s a little harder to spot. I’m pretty sure they will always wish my husband and I would divorce and split up custody to free them of each other’s company forever, but at least The Robot, as we’ve dubbed our system, gives them consistent snacks.

Meanwhile, I can take solace in one fact: That review was absolutely accurate, because not a single raccoon has gotten in these things.

Tech.title: Patreon is changing its algorithm to help smaller creators get discovered
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Patreon has announced a number of new and overhauled features that are designed to “build a better network – and a better internet,” according to CEO Jack Conte. The Patreon roadmap includes discovery algorithm updates, platform and security improvements, and new features for both creators and fans.

In a lengthy blog post, Conte outlines each of the changes and says they aim to address how the last generation of tech companies “have enshittified” by positioning Patreon as a better example of online creative and community platforms:

“The current version of the web is a failed promise for creators and fandoms. As creators, we can’t even reach our followers on the platforms anymore. Social media has created mass polarization, addiction, and made it increasingly difficult to build a creative community and business. I refuse to believe that this is the best way that the internet can work for creators and fans. I believe it can be better.”

The biggest change, according to Conte, is an overhaul of Patreon’s discovery algorithm. This will shift away from recommending creators based on who fans already follow — a system that favored suggesting larger creators — and will instead focus on comparing posts to other posts instead. The update will compare post content, including topic, style, craft, themes, and more, which Patreon believes will make it easier for smaller creators to get discovered.

Patreon is also introducing some short-form video features that can help the platform to better compete with TikTok and YouTube Shorts. There’s a Clips tool rolling out to iOS users that “automatically finds great moments” in long videos that creators can turn into short clips. These can be shared off platform, or on Patreon as Quips, the tweet-like feature Patreon introduced last year. Video previews and creator page layouts are also getting more customizable, and custom unblurred thumbnails can now be added to any public posts.

Clips is designed to help creators find the best snippets to turn into short-form videos. Image: Patreon

Additional updates in development include Niches, which are dedicated topic-based communities that sound like subreddits, alongside bolstered verification checks for user sign-in, and anti-scraping features to protect creators’ work from “AI thieves and scoundrels.” These are just the highlights of what has been announced, so check out Conte’s blog for full details of the roadmap.

Yup, that sure looks like a subreddit. Image: Patreon

Several of the updates announced are still in development and may not be fully released, subject to community feedback as they start to roll out for testing. This roadmap follows Patreon laying off 20 percent of its staff in January 2026. At the time, Conte said he doesn’t believe “AI replaces humans,” but that embracing the technology has “fundamentally transformed” how the company operates.

Tech.title: My big, fat, technophobic cat
Tech.content:
My cat Pablo is a voluptuous boy. His primordial pouch, originally thought to protect cats’ squishy insides, hangs low and wobbles to and fro. Once, when he was five or six, a vet sternly sat my spouse and me down, gravely stating, “He’s simply too young to be this fat.”

Pablo didn’t care, but we were traumatized. Now that he’s 10, the vets have repeatedly scolded us. All 20 pounds of his rotundity, they say, cannot continue. The specter of diabetes and kidney problems, and the fact that his obesity combined with a too-small pee-pee hole increases his risk of urinary crystals, mean that a diet is urgent.

I hear this every year. I keep saying “We are trying!!” The vets say, “Try harder! There are plenty of gadgets and toys you can use to stimulate enrichment, manage food, and encourage exercise!” What I don’t think the vets understand is that the state of pet tech is simply no match for Pablo.

As with humans, the key to weight loss in cats is a strict calorie deficit and increased activity. The problem is diets can be notoriously difficult for felines. Their small bodies don’t require that much food, spaying or neutering alters cat metabolisms, and they are famously finicky creatures. They’re also reliant on routines and, in Pablo’s case, can be heavily resistant to change.

His Royal Rotundity really is a sweet boy when I’m not making him pose for photos.

Pablo’s war on pet tech and diets all started with a Litter-Robot 4. We initially got it because Pablo’s poops were olfactory crimes. Manually scooping them was causing marital strife. (“He’s YOUR cat,” is what I’d say early on in our relationship. “He’s OUR cat,” my spouse retorted once we got married.)

Meanwhile, lifting Pablo onto one of our scales to monitor his weight would earn many yowls and skippity paps to the face. The Litter-Robot seemed like a clever solution because (1) automated scooping and (2) there’s a built-in scale. Whenever he does his business, I can log into the companion app to see how much he weighs (as well as monitor his bowel movements).

For a time, Pablo allowed us our folly. He was not a fan of the Litter-Robot. He eyed the spinning, globe-shaped bonnet with suspicion, but as a sophisticated, fancy boy, he wasn’t prone to pooping just anywhere. But then we moved to a four-story row home. My spouse and I viewed the three flights of stairs as a good chance for us, Pablo, and our other cat, Petey, to get in more steps. Three of us agreed. You can guess which one of us did not.

For logistical and cleaning purposes, we were not schlepping the Litter-Robot 4 up beyond the second floor. The thing weighs 24 pounds empty, and the thought of repeatedly carrying that up and down three flights of stairs to hose it down was too much. (It’s already bad enough that any litter box on an upper floor requires regularly carrying 15- to 30-pound bags of fresh litter up and down multiple flights.) In our previous apartments, we’d always put the Litter Robot, automated feeders, and pet fountains near the kitchen. But cats are territorial creatures. Before moving, Pablo and Petey shared spaces and litter boxes begrudgingly. With more space, they each established their own kingdoms. Pablo claimed the top floor — the bedroom. Petey claimed the second, where the Litter-Robot and the comfy couch reside. With the resulting borders settled into law, Pablo promptly stopped using the Litter-Robot. He also refuses to venture downstairs, except at 10PM each night to yell and enforce bedtime. We tried to encourage him to use the expensive poop robot anyway.

In protest, he began shitting on the carpet right outside my third-floor office door. The turd war continued for three weeks before we caved.

I’m not rich enough to buy a second Litter-Robot. The newest model costs $800, and while I enjoy a workout, the Litter-Robot 5 is even heavier at 28.7 pounds empty. So I bought a $20 stainless steel, not-very-smart litter box — and a smart pet scale designed to go under it. To save our noses, we put the litter box into one of those stealthy litter box enclosures that look like a regular credenza.

Pablo did not appreciate the new setup. At first, I thought he objected to his new pellet litter. We switched to an ultrafine microcrystal litter for his sensitive paws. He continued shitting outside my office. Turns out, he didn’t like that the under-box scale made the litter box enclosure feel cramped.

We removed it, and now I’m back to weighing him manually every few weeks.

Pablo 2, Tech 0.

Pablo only likes his catnip squirrel… …and his emotional support Squishmallow. Seen here is a pancaked Herbert.

Pablo doesn’t enjoy any form of movement that doesn’t end in a cuddle or treat. Ball tracks? Not a fan. The extremely cute Enabot robot? Icily ignored. We tried robot vacuums so he’d be forced to at least move rooms. Eventually, he started sitting on tables and chairs, watching disdainfully as the robovacs jammed themselves into furniture. Wand toys are viewed with snooty disgust. After a few half-hearted swats, he flops on his back and declares playtime over. He took one look at a cat tower and went, “Nah.” Pablo’s primary amusements are his catnip squirrel, pancaking his emotional support Squishmallows, and sometimes, if the mood strikes him, chasing a laser for three minutes. All he really wants is for me and my spouse to sit quietly with him on the bed, give him chin scratches, obey his strict sleeping schedule, and feed him on time.

Case in point, I sometimes test smart alarm clocks. But as I wrote in my review of the now-defunct Amazon Halo Rise, Pablo is an “affection eater.” This may seem absurd to non-cat owners, but some cats genuinely insist on company at mealtime. Pablo requires a witness, someone to sit on the floor next to him as he painstakingly eats each kibble bit one by one. (And to guard his meal from Petey.) He insists breakfast is promptly at 5:30AM, so when the automatic feeder goes off, I must sit with him for 10 to 15 minutes as he eats, occasionally redirecting Petey’s greedy face to his own bowl. He obviously doesn’t like any gadget that may encourage a variable wake-up time, such as a smart alarm clock that gently glows depending on sunrise times. He has knocked plenty off the nightstand, viewing his method of smothering me with his fluffy belly as superior.

After viewing some TikToks of cats enjoying walking pads, I called in a smart walking pad for review. Healthy for me, potentially healthy for my cats to get more steps in. Alas, this too ended up being a bust. I got stressed out by the smart features. Even the more mischievous Petey, with his one brain cell, could not process the concept of himself walking on the pad. All he did was bat at my feet while I walked on it. Pablo rolled off the belt when I tried putting him on it at a very low speed.

Pablo 6, Tech 0.

Bribes were required for these photos… ….but Pablo did not appreciate his little brother interrupting treat time.

In case you were wondering, Pablo also doesn’t consent to the pet surveillance state. He’s a handsome boy, but he hates getting his photo taken. Every single photo taken for this piece required bribes and cajoling. Most of the photos I have of him on my camera roll are of him sleeping, belly up. He’s learned to turn his head away from smartphone cameras. Petey now also does the same. So much so that my main use for smart glasses cameras is to get cute cat videos. (They have not yet learned what a white recording light is.)

I installed various pet cams because I was curious about how often Pablo was actually eating and moving around. I can also be a helicopter pet mom whenever we travel. But whereas Petey will purposefully mog for the pet cam, rolling around on the living room floor at 3AM like a demonic potato, Pablo will slink off into closets outside the camera’s field of view. I thought we outsmarted him by buying a fancy Petlibro automatic feeder with a built-in camera before a two-week vacation to Italy. Nope. We’d only just landed in Rome when, after checking in on the feed, we saw that the feeder had been knocked over.

I had to immediately call my pet sitter to go and cater to his whims.

Pablo 7, Tech 1 (I count the smart glasses as a win)

After eight years of technological warfare, however, there are two gadgets that Pablo tolerates — likes, even. One is the Petlibro cat fountain. He loves a fountain. The other is our Eight Sleep smart mattress cover. Like all cats, he loves a warm surface. So now, instead of climbing into a toasty bed every night, I have a staring contest with Pablo as he dares me to move him from my spot. I always win because I can just shove him over. But it’s not without some irritated meows and a lot of sass.

Pablo hates tech. (We also do not leave any uneaten food after supervised mealtime. That’s how he got so chonky to begin with.)

Pablo 7, Tech 3.

As for Pablo’s weight loss plan… The next obvious step would be RFID feeders to be 100 percent sure that Petey and Pablo aren’t overeating when we can’t supervise meals. You stick a collar with an RFID tag so that the feeder only allows a specific cat to eat. The only problem is they’re expensive, our current feeders aren’t broken, and Pablo hates collars. I have debated sticking a pet fitness tracker on Pablo. Ultimately, I decided against it because not only does he hate collars, but I already attempted it with my elderly Yorkie before she passed. The data tends to be more wellness-focused than actually useful for encouraging exercise.

Frankly, we adopted Petey because we thought a younger cat might encourage him to move around and play. Petey adores Pablo. The affection remains unrequited. My spouse has given up. Pablo is just destined to be round, they say. They constantly remind me that we already strictly control his food intake, and the pounds ain’t coming off.

I happen to think that maybe this is a Petey-and-tech problem. Perhaps a third kitten might do the trick.

Tech.title: Genki’s new customizable controller has a big screen and adjustable buttons
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After collaborating with 8BitDo on a gamepad two years ago, Genki launched the first controller the company designed from the ground up today. With an unorthodox design that positions its thumbsticks and buttons above a large 2.9-inch LCD screen, the Manta looks a lot chunkier than competing controllers. But what really sets it apart is a deeper focus on customizability with numerous settings that can be adjusted using the controller’s screen plus buttons and thumbsticks that can be tailored to each player’s preferences.

The Genki Manta is launching today through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign. The earliest backers can preorder the controller discounted to $189, while full retail pricing is expected to be $279. This is the company’s ninth crowdfunded device so while there’s always some risk with backing a Kickstarter, Genki has an excellent track record of delivering products this way.

While companies like Anbernic already have controllers with integrated screens, the Manta offers an especially deep level of customization through a settings interface powered by a dedicated Raspberry Pi RP2350 microcontroller. Players can configure and switch between multiple console, game, and user profiles, adjust thumbstick response and dead zones, increase the intensity of the haptic feedback, remap buttons, and record, edit, and combine multiple button presses to create custom macros.

The Manta includes two sets of oversized shoulder buttons and adjustable triggers with three different modes. Image: Genki

The Manta is one of the first controllers with what Genki calls “tristage triggers.” Many higher-end controllers already offer two switchable trigger modes that adjust the travel distance for racing or FPS games, but the Manta features a third in-between option the company claims is optimized for the “fastest repeated presses.” The controller’s face buttons are analog, too, and you can choose exactly how deep each button needs to travel before a press is detected to increase or decrease each one’s sensitivity.

The back of the Manta includes two pairs of programmable buttons. Image: Genki

Other features include linear magnetic ram motors in the grips that direct haptic feedback into your hands, drift-resistant tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) thumbsticks with adjustable tension, a 2,600mAh user-replaceable battery, and six additional remappable buttons located on the back and shoulders. The Manta even has a dedicated button for switching to a keyboard and mouse mode so you can navigate a browser without having to reach for another device. It can be used wirelessly over Bluetooth, but if latency is a concern, you can switch to using an included 2.4GHz dongle or connect directly to a console with a USB-C cable.

Tech.title: Google Discover is getting an AI chatbot-tuned feed
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google will soon allow you to customize your Discover feed by describing what you want to see. The new feature, rolling out to the Google app in the “coming days,” will use AI to automatically tweak your feed and “remember” your preferences for future visits.

You’ll find the option within the three-dot menu on your Discover feed. As shown in a video shared by Google, tapping the feature will open a chatbot-style interface, where you’ll be able to describe your preferences. The chatbot will confirm your choices and lay out the types of content it will prioritize, but you’ll also have the option to add more information if it doesn’t get it quite right. From there, you can hit “Refresh your feed” for the changes to take effect.

This might make it easier to control what you see in your Discover feed, which serves up recommended articles based on your activity across Google’s search engine and apps. Aside from Google Discover, several social media apps have added ways to customize your feeds with AI, including YouTube, Instagram, Bluesky, and X.

Google announced a couple of other changes as well, including the ability to personalize daily audio briefings in the Google News app on Android.

You can now choose the topics you want to hear about in your Google News audio briefing. Image: Google

There’s also an update to Preferred Sources, a feature that lets you see more of your favorite outlets across Search’s “top stories” section, AI Overviews, and AI Mode. With the change, publishers can place an interactive “Preferred Sources” button on their sites, which readers can select to quickly add it to their list without navigating away from the webpage.

Tech.title: Riot is ending development on its League of Legends fighting game
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Riot Games is already winding down work on 2XKO, the free-to-play League of Legends fighting game, less than a year after its initial launch. Riot says “active development” will conclude at the end of 2026 because the company hasn’t “seen enough players stick with the game to get to a path toward sustainability.” Servers will stay online “beyond 2026,” and Riot is unlocking all playable characters and refunding money spent on the game.

2XKO launched in an early access beta on PC in October 2025 and hit PS5 and Xbox Series X / S in January. But shortly after, Riot announced it would be cutting staff working on the game, saying at the time that “overall momentum hasn’t reached the level needed to support a team of this size long term.”

It seems like things never turned a corner. Riot says in its Thursday announcement that it evaluated the game’s overall performance through the year, and while there were some bright spots with new character releases and competitive events, it wasn’t enough to keep the game going. “Even in these highlight moments, however, we saw no meaningful, sustained change in 2XKO’s trajectory; only a fraction of what it would take to trend toward sustainability,” Riot says. “Over time it became clear it would be impossible for us to continue actively developing the game as we are today.”

Riot says it would have continued development if “we saw any viable future,” but notes that “2XKO costs us substantially more to operate than it brings in, and engagement has stayed relatively flat despite our larger updates.”

2XKO is just the latest big live service bet that hasn’t panned out. Just this week, Bloomberg reported that Sony is stripping live service elements from its in-development multiplayer Horizon title. Highguard, following its closing announcement at December’s Game Awards, permanently shut down less than two months after launch. Earlier this year, Remedy announced a final major update for FBC: Firebreak, its live service shooter set in the Control universe — though like Riot’s plan for 2XKO, Remedy has chosen to keep Firebreak online. Even Fortnite isn’t immune to problems, as developer Epic Games laid off staff in March following a “downturn in Fortnite engagement.”

Tech.title: The Genesis GV90 blows the bloody doors off what’s possible in EV design
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Genesis, Hyundai’s luxury brand, just revealed its first full-size, three-row electric SUV for the US market, the GV90. And arguably it has some of the wildest designs and features in the auto market today.

Right off the bat, the coach-style doors signal that things aren’t what they seem with the GV90. When the front and rear doors open outward, the B-pillar disappears, creating an extra-large opening into the vehicle — because you’re the kind of person who can afford it.

Genesis is calling it the Neolun Arch Gate, “the world’s first independently opening and closing hidden B-pillar coach door.” But it’s more than just that.

To be sure, as the middle post between the front and back doors, the B-pillar is critical for vehicle safety. This is the vertical metal support needed as reinforcement against roof collapses during rollover. The B pillar also absorbs crash energy during a T-bone collision. And here’s Genesis being like, “What if we got rid of it for the biggest possible entrance into the vehicle?” That’s wild.

Previous Next





1 / 4

Thankfully, Genesis doesn’t dismiss the safety implications of a B-pillar-less vehicle. The company claims to have created a new structure that “seamlessly marries the doors to the vehicle body while maintaining the highest safety standards.” It replaces the B-pillar with “high-strength dual steel beams” selected for their rigidity that joins the doors and body and “effectively disperses collision forces.” Here’s more on that:

A concealed yet robust roll cage is created by reinforcing the passenger cabin with a frame 1.5 times thicker than conventional vehicles and fortifying it with integrated high-strength steel tubes and structural foam. This hidden roll cage structure protects occupants while achieving crash safety performance equivalent to vehicles with conventional B-pillars.

Whether or not this meets the standards for safety will be up to the regulators and third-party groups that test these things for a living. If the GV90 passes its crash tests with flying colors, we’ll know that the new architecture works. And that really could open up a new door (pun definitely intended) of what’s possible with vehicle designs. If it fails those tests, the GV90 could become a footnote in the book on misguided vehicle designs (right next to the Fiat Multipla, with its two-tiered upper cabin that made it look like a car stacked on top of another car).

Genesis didn’t stop at coach doors, though. The front seats can rotate 180 degrees to face the second row, creating a lounge-like environment. This was a feature found commonly in early autonomous vehicle designs, but rarely seen in a production-intent vehicle. The idea was that when we didn’t have to drive the vehicle ourselves, we could sit facing our fellow passengers, like we’re riding in a 19th-century stagecoach. Zoox used this idea in its purpose-built robotaxis — and now Genesis is bringing the idea to its flagship SUV. Of course, Genesis intends for the seats to be rotated only when parked, not while driving.

Previous Next





1 / 4

Inside, you’ll find a 23.6-inch OLED Cinematic Display that can rise 90 millimeters and expand into a 24.6-inch display. There’s also a 25-inch heads-up display to replace the conventional instrument cluster, and it displays details like speed, navigation, and driver assist levels. And speaking of driver assist, there’s a feature called Memory Reversing Assist that remembers the vehicle’s path and can automatically guide it backward out of narrow alleys or parking spots.

The regular EV stuff is almost the least interesting part about this SUV. The GV90 rides on a 123.5kWh battery with 800 nominal volts controlled by a wireless battery management system. It feeds power to two electric drive units, each with its own electronically controlled limited-slip differential for a combined power output of 657 horsepower and 590lb-ft of torque. It supports 350kW DC fast charging, but the estimated range is only 310 miles.

Back to the cavalcade of whimsy. You’ve heard of heated seats. But what about heated floors? Or heated armrests, side panels, and door trims? There’s massaging seats with 15 individual air bladders, and a heated windshield that uses a thin metallic coating to remove winter frost without having to rely on climate control. And a roof airbag. An airbag for your roof. An airbag that covers the entire glass roof and protects you in case of rollover. Roof airbag.

There are other phrases in this announcement that are equally difficult to wrap one’s head around. But I think what’s clear is that Genesis is trying to do it all. In an age of EV pessimism in the US, in which other automakers are retreating to their corners and trying to recalibrate for affordability and profitability, Genesis is saying, “Fuck everything, we’re doing five blades.”

Tech.title: Tesla, Uber, and Waymo all get the OK to operate thousands of robotaxis in Nevada
Tech.content:
Nevada, get ready for the robotaxis.

The Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved three permits Thursday that will allow Tesla, Uber, and Waymo to operate commercial robotaxi services in Clark County, home to Las Vegas. Together, these permits would deploy up to 8,000 robotaxis across the county over the next 12 months.

Tesla’s permit allows it to deploy up to 5,000 robotaxis, while Waymo is allowed operate up to 1,000 autonomous vehicles over the next year. Uber was also approved for 1,000 robotaxis, which it will operate through partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox. Zoox already holds an autonomous vehicle network company permit that allows it to operate 100 robotaxis.

Whether these companies will be able to launch that many robotaxis is an unanswered question. Testimony from Tesla representatives and the other companies suggests the answer is no.

“The 5,000 has always been a ceiling for us,” said Eric Early, Tesla’s Cybercab chief engineer, during the meeting. “I don’t think we’ll be in a position by this time next year to deploy 5,000 vehicles, and it’s not [because of] the technology. … I think we would be extremely happy and satisfied if we could get ourselves up to 2,500, maybe a bit higher than that in the next year.”

Even if these three companies roll out only half of those totals, Clark County — and Las Vegas specifically — is shaping up to be a major robotaxi battleground, with Tesla, Uber (via its autonomous vehicle partners Motional and Zoox), and Waymo all competing for the same riders.

That kind of fast, large-scale robotaxi deployment is poised to change the city — and specifically its workforce. Depending on who you ask, these companies will either deliver a whole new category of jobs designed to maintain, charge, and clean these vehicles or will wipe out an entire category of workers: human taxi and gig drivers.

Representatives from the Livery Operators Association and local taxi companies opposed the permits, arguing the approvals move too far, too fast.

“These applications raise two grave concerns,” said Kimberly Maxson-Rushton, a lawyer representing the Livery Operators Association, at the hearing. “One deals with the oversaturation of the commercial transportation industry as a whole in Nevada,” she said. “And the second one deals with the overcrowding of the roadways, and specifically the Golden Triangle.”

The Golden Triangle, an area between the airport and Las Vegas Boulevard and the surrounding area, is where most of the AV testing has occurred to date. Motional is also testing in the downtown area and in a shopping district known as Town Square.

Uber has tried to position itself as the Goldilocks option in this fight, advocating for a hybrid approach in which ride-hailing networks are made up of humans and robotaxis. The company has even lobbied for a system that would require robotaxis to operate on a ride-hailing network that also uses human drivers, a stance that puts it at odds with Waymo and doubles as a hedge against its own autonomous ambitions falling short of Tesla’s or Waymo’s.

Uber made a similar pitch during the NTA meeting, noting that a hybrid approach would allow cities to gradually integrate vehicles to meet peak demand rather than flooding the market all at once.

Tech.title: AI data startup Micro1 reaches $500M gross run rate amid AI training boom
Tech.content:
The near-bottomless demand for unique AI training data from top labs and corporations is driving a massive boom for a cohort of data-labeling startups.

One of these fast-growing businesses is Micro1, a four-year-old startup that expanded its gross annual run rate from $100 million to $500 million over the past eight months, according to a person familiar with the company. Like its peers that hire domain experts such as doctors, lawyers, and scientists on a contract basis, Micro1 retains roughly 60% to 70% of that figure, putting its net annual run rate between $150 million and $200 million.

While Micro1 still lags competitors like Mercor (which hit $2 billion in gross annualized revenue this summer) and Handshake (which reached $1 billion earlier this year), the startup’s revenue growth shows that there is more than enough demand to support multiple players supplying AI training data.

The rapid growth is bound to continue, with some researchers hypothesizing that future AI spending on data could rival spending on compute.

That outlook bodes well for Micro1, which is seeing its contract sizes grow at an accelerated pace and expects its margins to expand over time. The startup is increasingly generating synthetic data without human involvement, such as by creating automated descriptions of video content. Additionally, some of the data it generates can be sold to multiple customers, driving gross margins for this “off-the-shelf” data as high as 80% to 90%, a person familiar with the startup’s finances told TechCrunch.

Selling the same datasets to multiple clients has sparked recent controversy, with critics arguing that distributing off-the-shelf data to Chinese AI developers helps make their models as powerful as top U.S. models.

Micro1’s founder, Ali Ansari, said last month on X that unlike some of its competitors, the startup doesn’t sell its data to Chinese model makers. “Some human data companies work with foreign adversaries. [A]nd the results show today in Kimi K3. We believe it’s shameful to claim American AI dominance desires while selling millions worth of data to countries that we are in adversarial competition with.”

Like Mercor, Micro1 began as an AI recruiting startup. But after noticing that data-labeling clients were using his AI platform to vet and recruit engineers for annotation, Ansari decided to pivot and enter the data-labeling business, too.

Ansari previously told TechCrunch that in addition to having its experts evaluate model outputs — a concept known as reinforcement learning gyms — the company is building a robotics pre-training dataset by having hundreds of generalists record everyday object interactions in their homes.

Micro1 raised its Series A at a $500 million valuation last September, and TechCrunch understands that the startup may have recently raised another round at a significantly higher valuation.

Micro1 didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Learn what VCs actually want, from a founder who’s raised $1B
Tech.content:
Loading the player…

Investors want founders who understand the financial reality of their business. Messy data, misunderstood metrics, or waiting until you’re nearly out of cash to start fundraising can cost founders leverage, valuation, and even a term sheet.

In this episode of Build Mode, host Isabelle Johannessen sits down with Sasha Orloff, founder and CEO of Puzzle and Startup Battlefield alum, to talk about what he’s learned from building companies that have raised more than $1 billion collectively.

Sasha breaks down what investors look for during fundraising, which financial metrics founders should know by heart, and why VCs don’t expect your startup to be perfect — they just expect you to understand its reality. He also shares how he nearly lost a term sheet because his data room wasn’t ready, how fundraising diligence changes as a startup grows, and why getting your financial house in order can help founders raise with more confidence and leverage.

They get into:

What raising more than $1 billion across multiple companies taught Sasha about fundraising.

Why investors value founders who have a strong grasp of their company’s financial reality.

The financial metrics founders should know before pitching VCs.

How investor expectations change from pre-seed and seed through Series A, B, and beyond.

Why revenue growth and the quality of that revenue are critical fundraising metrics.

How runway, margins, sales efficiency, and profitability factor into investor decisions.

Why waiting until you’re running out of cash can hurt your fundraising leverage.

How Sasha nearly lost a term sheet because his data room wasn’t ready.

Why financial organization and compliance can influence investor confidence and startup valuations.

What founders should have prepared for the due diligence process.

Why VCs don’t expect perfection — and why being honest about what isn’t working can make for a stronger pitch.

How Sasha’s own fundraising and finance frustrations ultimately led him to build Puzzle.

How AI could change the way startups manage accounting and understand their financial health.
